*   I think the only way you can successfully be a mum and an actress is by not carrying around the burden of the character. Between the time the director says "Action" and "Cut," it's all true for me. But when I stop saying the lines, it's not true anymore.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Rachel Weiss (Perth)](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)&redirect=no "Rachel Weiss (Perth)"))

British counsellor, teacher and social entrepreneur

Not to be confused with [Rachel Weisz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz "Rachel Weisz").

**Rachel Weiss** (born 1966) is British counsellor, [teacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teacher "Teacher") and [social entrepreneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_entrepreneurship "Social entrepreneurship") based in [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland"), [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland"), who set up the [Menopause Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menopause_Caf%C3%A9 "Menopause Café") model which has become a global movement.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:1-1) Starting from the first café in Perth in 2017, there are now cafés across the world that promote conversation about [menopause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menopause "Menopause"). She has received the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom")’s Point of Light Award 2018[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:3-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-3) and the Association of Scottish Businesswomen (ASB) Lifetime Achievement Award 2024.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:0-4)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Weiss was born in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in 1966. Her virologist father [Robin Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Weiss "Robin Weiss") was born in London to [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany")[Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews") refugees. Her mother, a maths teacher, had moved to the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") from [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore "Singapore") in the 1960s.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:1-1)

Weiss won a scholarship to work as a [computer programmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programmer "Programmer"), at what is now [Plymouth Marjon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Marjon_University "Plymouth Marjon University"), before attending [the University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") to study [Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics "Mathematics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:1-1)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:2-5) Weiss moved to the [University of Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh "University of Edinburgh") for her postgraduate study in [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), obtaining a [MSc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") in 1990. She then undertook teaching training in Northern College, [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen") (now part of the [University of Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Aberdeen "University of Aberdeen")).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-6)

She met her husband Andy in Edinburgh and moved to Perth in 1997. They have three children.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Charitable work and volunteering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Charitable work and volunteering")]

While at Oxford, Weiss formed the Homeless Action Group society, organising a rota for students to volunteer in homeless shelters.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:2-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-8) After graduation, she volunteered with a charity supporting refugees in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), teaching Maths and English to [Lebanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_people "Lebanese people") refugees.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-9)

### Teaching and counselling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Teaching and counselling")]

After teacher training in Aberdeen, Weiss worked as a maths teacher and a tutor at the [Open University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_University "Open University"). She undertook a counselling course, as she felt this would make her a better teacher, but it influenced another career change.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:5-10) In 1997, Weiss and Christine Partridge founded Rowan Consultancy, an organisation providing counselling and workplace support services..[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:5-10)

### Menopause Café charity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Menopause Café charity")]

At the age of 50, Weiss saw a TV documentary about menopause presented by [Kirsty Wark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsty_Wark "Kirsty Wark"), _The_ _Menopause and Me_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]She was inspired to create the first Menopause Café using the format of the [Death Café](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Cafe "Death Cafe"), which she had previously hosted in Perth.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The first café was in June 2017, held in Blend Coffee Lounge, Perth with nearly 30 people in attendance.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:4-11) In its first year, more than 38 café events were held in Scotland, [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada").It became a registered charity in 2018 and Kirsty Wark became their Patron.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:3-2) People Magazine called it a "global movement" in 2023.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-12) Weiss set up the annual Menopause Festival, called Flushfest, in 2018.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:4-11)

[Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)")[MSP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Scottish_Parliament "Member of the Scottish Parliament")[Monica Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monica_Lennon "Monica Lennon") contacted Weiss in 2022 to discuss menopause in the workplace stating "_Governments need to think about what a good, modern workplace looks like, where it is not taboo to talk about menstruation and menopause leave_."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-13)

## What is a menopause café?

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: What is a menopause café?")]

A Menopause Café is a pop-up, [not-for-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not-For-Profit "Not-For-Profit") discussion group, usually in a local café or workplace, with volunteers facilitating, where everyone either new or returning, talks about menopause over a cuppa and cake. The ethos of the events is to provide a confidential space, where people can learn, share ideas, experiences and information around living with menopause regardless of age or gender.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:4-11)

## Awards and recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weiss_(businesswoman)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Awards and recognition")]

*   2018 – UK Points of Light Award, Prime Minister’s Office[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:3-2)

*   2024 – Lifetime Achievement Award, Association of Scottish Businesswomen (ASB)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weiss_(Perth)#cite_note-:0-4)

**Rachel Wyse** (born 22 January 1985)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Watch-1) is an Irish [journalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalist "Journalist"), [presenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_presenter "News presenter"), former [Sky Sports News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Sports_News "Sky Sports News") anchor and equestrian [show jumper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_jumping "Show jumping").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Wyse&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Wyse attended [St Andrew's College, Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Andrew's_College,_Dublin "St Andrew's College, Dublin").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-2) She graduated from the [Institute of Art, Design and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BAn_Laoghaire_Institute_of_Art,_Design_and_Technology "Dún Laoghaire Institute of Art, Design and Technology") in [Dún Laoghaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BAn_Laoghaire "Dún Laoghaire") with a degree in Business Studies and Arts Management.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Assets-3)

## Television career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Wyse&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Television career")]

Wyse eventually moved into television, producing and presenting her own entertainment and cultural programme on the [City Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Channel "City Channel").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-4)

She moved into sports presenting with the _Show Jumping Ireland Premier Series_ in 2008 & 2009 on [Sky Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Sports "Sky Sports"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Watch-1)[Horse & Country TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_&_Country_TV "Horse & Country TV") and [TG4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TG4 "TG4"), and was the face of [Leinster Rugby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leinster_Rugby "Leinster Rugby")'s online television channel Leinster Rugby TV.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Wyse then became a co-presenter on [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland "Republic of Ireland")'s only domestic motoring show[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-5)_Xccelerate_ on [3E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3e "3e").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Watch-1)

In July 2010, Wyse was offered a contract with [Sky Sports News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Sports_News "Sky Sports News")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Assets-3) and made her first appearance on the channel the same month.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Watch-1) She worked full-time as a Sky Sports News Anchor. Wyse has filmed special reports with Olympic boxer [Katie Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katie_Taylor "Katie Taylor"), Irish international rugby player [Brian O'Driscoll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_O'Driscoll "Brian O'Driscoll") and Manchester United player [Juan Mata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Mata "Juan Mata"), as well as reporting from the London Olympics 2012 and Wimbledon.

In May 2014, Wyse was announced as a presenter of Sky Sports's new coverage of [Gaelic games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_games "Gaelic games"). Sky purchased the broadcasting rights for Championship [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_football "Gaelic football") and [hurling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurling "Hurling") from the [GAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaelic_Athletic_Association "Gaelic Athletic Association").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-7)

Wyse parted company with [Sky Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Sports "Sky Sports") in February 2021, after eleven years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-8)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Wyse&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

She became engaged to showjumper [Tim Gredley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Gredley "Tim Gredley") on 5 February 2018.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-9) They were married on 12 January 2019 with a reception at [Adare Manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adare_Manor "Adare Manor") in [Co Limerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Limerick "County Limerick").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-10)

On 8 March 2020, Wyse announced she and her husband were expecting their first child.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-11) On 24 July 2020, she gave birth to a baby girl called Isabella.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-12) The couple welcomed their second child, a daughter named Charlotte in December 2021.

## Sports career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Wyse&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Sports career")]

She competed internationally for Ireland as part of two [European Show Jumping Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Show_Jumping_Championships "European Show Jumping Championships") teams[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-Assets-3) and has competed on the Irish National circuit.

On St. Patrick's Day 2011, Wyse rode Silent Jo at [Cheltenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham_Racecourse "Cheltenham Racecourse") in the charity race for [Cancer Research UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer_Research_UK "Cancer Research UK"). She raised more than £60,000 for the charity.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-13) She was invited to the House of Lords to receive recognition as one of Cancer Research UK's top fundraisers in 2011.

Wyse has a Saturday column in the _[Irish Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish\_Independent "Irish Independent")_, WYSE ON SPORT, which contains opinion pieces covering all sports.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Wyse#cite_note-14)

**Rachel Hannah Weisz** ([/v aɪ s/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English");[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-2) born 7 March 1970)[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-birthplace-9) is a British actress. Known for her roles in [independent films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_films "Independent films") and [blockbusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster_(entertainment) "Blockbuster (entertainment)"), she has received [several awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Rachel_Weisz "List of awards and nominations received by Rachel Weisz"), including an [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award "Academy Award"), a [British Academy Film Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy_Film_Award "British Academy Film Award"), a [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award "Golden Globe Award"), a [Screen Actors Guild Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild_Award "Screen Actors Guild Award"), and a [Laurence Olivier Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier_Award "Laurence Olivier Award").

Weisz began acting in stage and television productions in the early 1990s, and made her film debut in _[Death Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_Machine "Death Machine")_ (1994). She won a [Critics' Circle Theatre Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critics'_Circle_Theatre_Award "Critics' Circle Theatre Award") for her role in the 1994 revival of [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward")'s play _[Design for Living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design\_for\_Living "Design for Living")_, and went on to appear in the 1999 [Donmar Warehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donmar_Warehouse "Donmar Warehouse") production of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams")' drama _[Suddenly Last Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suddenly\_Last\_Summer "Suddenly Last Summer")_. Her film breakthrough came with her starring role as [Evelyn Carnahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Carnahan "Evelyn Carnahan") in the Hollywood action films _[The Mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_(1999\_film) "The Mummy (1999 film)")_ (1999) and _[The Mummy Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_Returns "The Mummy Returns")_ (2001).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-hollywood_debut-10) Weisz went on to star in several films of the 2000s, including _[Enemy at the Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy\_at\_the\_Gates "Enemy at the Gates")_ (2001), _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_ (2002), _[Runaway Jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runaway\_Jury "Runaway Jury")_ (2003), _[Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine\_(film) "Constantine (film)")_ (2005), _[The Fountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fountain "The Fountain")_ (2006), _[Definitely, Maybe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definitely,\_Maybe "Definitely, Maybe")_ (2008), _[The Lovely Bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lovely\_Bones\_(film) "The Lovely Bones (film)")_ (2009) and _[The Whistleblower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Whistleblower "The Whistleblower")_ (2010).

For her performance as an activist in the 2005 thriller _[The Constant Gardener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Constant\_Gardener\_(film) "The Constant Gardener (film)")_, she won the [Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress"), and for playing [Blanche DuBois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_DuBois "Blanche DuBois") in a 2009 revival of _[A Streetcar Named Desire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Streetcar\_Named\_Desire "A Streetcar Named Desire")_, she won the [Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier_Award_for_Best_Actress "Laurence Olivier Award for Best Actress"). In the 2010s, Weisz continued to star in big-budget films such as the action film _[The Bourne Legacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bourne\_Legacy\_(film) "The Bourne Legacy (film)")_ (2012) and the fantasy film _[Oz the Great and Powerful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oz\_the\_Great\_and\_Powerful "Oz the Great and Powerful")_ (2013) and achieved critical acclaim for her performances in the independent films _[The Deep Blue Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Deep\_Blue\_Sea\_(2011\_film) "The Deep Blue Sea (2011 film)")_ (2011), _[Denial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denial\_(2016\_film) "Denial (2016 film)")_ (2016), and _[The Favourite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Favourite\_(2018\_film) "The Favourite (2018 film)")_ (2018). For her portrayal of [Sarah Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Churchill,_Duchess_of_Marlborough "Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough") in _The Favourite_, she won the [BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role") and received a second Academy Award nomination.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-11) Weisz portrayed [Melina Vostokoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melina_Vostokoff_(Marvel_Cinematic_Universe) "Melina Vostokoff (Marvel Cinematic Universe)") in the [Marvel Cinematic Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Cinematic_Universe "Marvel Cinematic Universe") film _[Black Widow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Widow\_(2021\_film) "Black Widow (2021 film)")_ (2021) and starred as twin obstetricians in the thriller miniseries _[Dead Ringers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Ringers\_(miniseries) "Dead Ringers (miniseries)")_ (2023).

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Weisz was born on 7 March 1970 in [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster "Westminster"), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), and grew up in [Hampstead Garden Suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampstead_Garden_Suburb "Hampstead Garden Suburb").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-12) In 1938, before [WW2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WW2 "WW2"), her parents as children had come to the UK to escape the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazis "Nazis").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-16) Her father, George Weisz, was a [Hungarian Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Jewish "Hungarian Jewish") mechanical engineer and inventor known for pioneering a type of [ventilator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ventilator "Ventilator").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-19) Her mother, Edith Ruth ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Teich),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-20) was a teacher, and later a psychotherapist, originally from [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), Austria.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-thisislondon-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-22) Her maternal grandfather's ancestry was [Austrian Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Jewish "Austrian Jewish"); her maternal grandmother was [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic "Catholic") and of Italian ancestry.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-27) The scholar and [social activist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_activist "Social activist")[James Parkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Parkes_(priest) "James Parkes (priest)") helped her mother's family to leave Austria for England.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-People-Denial-2016-28) Weisz's mother was raised in the Catholic church and formally [converted to Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Converted_to_Judaism "Converted to Judaism") upon marrying Weisz's father.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-theguardian.com-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-naie-30) Weisz's maternal grandfather was Alexander Teich, a Jewish activist who had been a secretary of the [World Union of Jewish Students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Union_of_Jewish_Students "World Union of Jewish Students").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-llev-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-rasl-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-mrp-33)

Her younger sister [Minnie Weisz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_Weisz "Minnie Weisz") is a [visual artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-art_photography "Fine-art photography").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-34) Weisz's parents valued the arts; they encouraged their children to form opinions of their own by engaging their participation in family debates.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-talk-35) Weisz left [North London Collegiate School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_London_Collegiate_School "North London Collegiate School") and attended [Benenden School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benenden_School "Benenden School") for one year, completing her [A-levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level "A-level") at [St Paul's Girls School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_Girls_School "St Paul's Girls School").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-Yahoo-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-37)

Known for being an "[English rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_rose_(epithet) "English rose (epithet)")",[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-HelloMagazine-40)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-theguardian.com-29) Weisz began modelling at the age of 14.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-41) In 1984, she gained public attention when she turned down an offer to star in _[King David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King\_David\_(film) "King David (film)")_ with [Richard Gere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Gere "Richard Gere").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-Yahoo-36)

In 1988, Weisz went up to [Trinity Hall, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Hall,_Cambridge "Trinity Hall, Cambridge"), taking a [2:1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2:1 "2:1") in [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literary_studies "English literary studies"). At Trinity Hall, she was a contemporary of [Sacha Baron Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacha_Baron_Cohen "Sacha Baron Cohen"), [Alexander Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Armstrong "Alexander Armstrong"), [Emily Maitlis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Maitlis "Emily Maitlis"), [Sue Perkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Perkins "Sue Perkins"), [Mel Giedroyc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Giedroyc "Mel Giedroyc"), [Richard Osman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Osman "Richard Osman") and [Ben Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Miller "Ben Miller") (whom she dated briefly).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-42) She appeared in student plays, co-founding an all-female student drama group _Cambridge Talking Tongues_.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-43) The group won a _Guardian_ Student Drama Award at the 1991 [Edinburgh Festival Fringe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Festival_Fringe "Edinburgh Festival Fringe") for an improvised two-woman–show piece written by Weisz herself called _Slight Possession_,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-ncg-44) directed by David Farr.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-45)

Weisz then trained under master clown [Philippe Gaulier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Gaulier "Philippe Gaulier") at [École Philippe Gaulier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_Philippe_Gaulier "École Philippe Gaulier").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-47)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In 1992, Weisz appeared in the television film _Advocates II_, followed by roles in the _[Inspector Morse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector\_Morse\_(TV\_series) "Inspector Morse (TV series)")_ episode "[Twilight of the Gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_of_the_Gods_(Inspector_Morse) "Twilight of the Gods (Inspector Morse)")", and the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s steamy period drama _[Scarlet and Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlet\_and\_Black\_(TV\_series) "Scarlet and Black (TV series)")_, alongside [Ewan McGregor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ewan_McGregor "Ewan McGregor").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-MSNF-48)_Dirty Something_, a BBC Screen Two, hour-long television film made in 1992, was Weisz's first film.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-49)

Weisz's breakthrough role on the stage was that of Gilda in [Sean Mathias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Mathias "Sean Mathias")'s 1994 revival of [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward")'s _[Design for Living](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design\_for\_Living "Design for Living")_ at the [Gielgud Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gielgud_Theatre "Gielgud Theatre"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-esu-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-wen-51) for which she received the London Critics' Circle Award for the most promising newcomer.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-53) Her portrayal was described as "wonderful" by a contemporary review.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-54)

Weisz started her film career with a minor role in the 1994 film _[Death Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death\_Machine "Death Machine")_;[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-MSNF-48) her first major role came in the 1996 film _[Chain Reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain\_Reaction\_(1996\_film) "Chain Reaction (1996 film)")_.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-55) The film received mostly negative reviews–it holds a 16% rating on [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes")[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-56) and was a minor financial success.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-57) She next appeared as Miranda Fox in _[Stealing Beauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stealing\_Beauty "Stealing Beauty")_, directed by [Bernardo Bertolucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernardo_Bertolucci "Bernardo Bertolucci"),[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-58) where she was first labelled an "English rose".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-HelloMagazine-40)

Weisz found roles in the 1997 American drama _[Swept from the Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swept\_from\_the\_Sea "Swept from the Sea")_,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-59) the 1998 British television comedy-drama _[My Summer with Des](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Summer\_with\_Des "My Summer with Des")_, [Michael Winterbottom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Winterbottom "Michael Winterbottom")'s crime film _[I Want You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Want\_You\_(1998\_film) "I Want You (1998 film)")_,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-indmagaz-60) and [David Leland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leland "David Leland")'s _[The Land Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Land\_Girls "The Land Girls")_, based on [Angela Huth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Huth "Angela Huth")'s book of the same name.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-61)

In 1999, Weisz played Greta in the historical film _[Sunshine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunshine\_(1999\_film) "Sunshine (1999 film)")_.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-62) The same year, her international breakthrough came with the 1999 adventure film _[The Mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_(1999\_film) "The Mummy (1999 film)")_, in which she played the female lead opposite [Brendan Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Fraser "Brendan Fraser"). Her character, Evelyn Carnahan, is an English [Egyptologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptologist "Egyptologist"),[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-63) who undertakes an expedition to the fictional ancient Egyptian city of Hamunaptra to discover an ancient book. _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ criticised the direction of the film, writing: "(the actors) have been directed to broad, undisciplined performances [...] Buffoonery hardly seems like Weisz's natural domain, as the actress strains for comic effects that she can't achieve".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-64) She followed this up with the sequel _[The Mummy Returns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_Returns "The Mummy Returns")_ in 2001, which grossed an estimated $433 million worldwide,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-65) (equivalent to $787 million in 2025 dollars)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-inflation-US-66) higher than the original's $260 million[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-67) (equal to $502 million in 2025 dollars).[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-inflation-US-66)

Also in 1999, she played the role of Catherine in the [Donmar Warehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donmar_Warehouse "Donmar Warehouse") production of [Tennessee Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams")' _[Suddenly Last Summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suddenly\_Last\_Summer "Suddenly Last Summer")_,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-autogenerated1-68)_What's on Stage_ called her "captivating", stating that she brought "a degree of credibility to a difficult part".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-69) In 2001, Weisz appeared in [Neil LaBute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_LaBute "Neil LaBute")'s _[The Shape of Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shape\_of\_Things "The Shape of Things")_ at the [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre"), then temporarily located in London's [King's Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Cross,_London "King's Cross, London"), for which she received a [Theatre World Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_World_Award "Theatre World Award").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-shape-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-71) CurtainUp called her "a sophisticated, independent artist" with "great stage presence".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-72)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2000s")]

In 2000, she portrayed Petula in the film _[Beautiful Creatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beautiful\_Creatures\_(2000\_film) "Beautiful Creatures (2000 film)")_,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-MSNF-48) followed by her portrayal of [Tania Chernova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_Chernova "Tania Chernova") in 2001's _[Enemy at the Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy\_at\_the\_Gates "Enemy at the Gates")_,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-73) and the 2002 comedy-drama _[About a Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About\_a\_Boy\_(film) "About a Boy (film)")_, with [Hugh Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Grant "Hugh Grant"), based on [Nick Hornby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hornby "Nick Hornby")'s 1998 [novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/About_a_Boy_(novel) "About a Boy (novel)").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-74) In 2003, she played Marlee in the adaptation of [John Grisham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Grisham "John Grisham")'s legal thriller novel _[The Runaway Jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Runaway\_Jury "The Runaway Jury")_;[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-75) and starred in the film adaptation of the romantic comedy-drama play _[The Shape of Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shape\_of\_Things "The Shape of Things")_.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-76)

### 2010s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2010s")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Rachel_Weisz_2012.jpg/250px-Rachel_Weisz_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rachel_Weisz_2012.jpg)

Weisz at the 2012 [Deauville American Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deauville_American_Film_Festival "Deauville American Film Festival")

Weisz starred in the film _[The Whistleblower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Whistleblower "The Whistleblower")_, which debuted at the [Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_International_Film_Festival "Toronto International Film Festival") in 2010. The film was based on the [true story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DynCorp#Employee_involvement_in_child_sex_slave_traffic "DynCorp") of human trafficking by employees of contractor [DynCorp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DynCorp "DynCorp"). During its première, the intense depiction of the treatment meted out to victims by the kidnappers made a woman in the audience faint.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-101)_Variety_ wrote "Weisz's performance holds the viewer every step of the way."[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-102) That same year, she guest-starred in the animated series _[The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons "The Simpsons")_, in the [22nd season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_22 "The Simpsons season 22") episode "[How Munched is That Birdie in the Window?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_Munched_is_That_Birdie_in_the_Window%3F "How Munched is That Birdie in the Window?")".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-103) Weisz's 2011 roles included an adaptation of [Terence Rattigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence_Rattigan "Terence Rattigan")'s play _[The Deep Blue Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Deep\_Blue\_Sea\_(2011\_film) "The Deep Blue Sea (2011 film)")_,[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-104)[Fernando Meirelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Meirelles "Fernando Meirelles")' drama _[360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/360\_(film) "360 (film)")_,[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-105) the BBC espionage thriller _[Page Eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page\_Eight "Page Eight")_, and the thriller film _[Dream House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream\_House\_(2011\_film) "Dream House (2011 film)")_.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-106)

She filmed scenes for _[To the Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To\_the\_Wonder "To the Wonder")_, a 2012 romantic drama film written and directed by [Terrence Malick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrence_Malick "Terrence Malick"); her scenes were cut.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-108)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-109) She has starred in the 2012 action thriller film _[The Bourne Legacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Bourne\_Legacy\_(film) "The Bourne Legacy (film)")_ based on the series of books by [Robert Ludlum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Ludlum "Robert Ludlum").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-110)

In 2013, Weisz starred on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") alongside her husband, [Daniel Craig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig"), in a revival of [Harold Pinter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Pinter "Harold Pinter")'s _[Betrayal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betrayal\_(play) "Betrayal (play)")_. It opened 27 October 2013, and closed 5 January 2014.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-112) Box office receipts of $17.5 million made it the second highest grossing Broadway play of 2013.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-113) That year, Weisz played [Evanora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wicked_Witch_of_the_East "Wicked Witch of the East") in the fantasy film _[Oz the Great and Powerful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oz\_the\_Great\_and\_Powerful "Oz the Great and Powerful")_.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-114)

Weisz at the [2015 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Cannes_Film_Festival "2015 Cannes Film Festival")

In 2015, she appeared in drama film _[Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth\_(2015\_film) "Youth (2015 film)")_ and in science fiction film _[The Lobster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lobster "The Lobster")_. _Lobster_ won the Cannes Jury Prize. In 2016, she appeared in the drama film _[The Light Between Oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Light\_Between\_Oceans\_(film) "The Light Between Oceans (film)")_, and portrayed Holocaust historian [Deborah Lipstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_Lipstadt "Deborah Lipstadt") in _[Denial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denial\_(2016\_film) "Denial (2016 film)")_, a film based on Lipstadt's book, and directed by [Mick Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Jackson_(director) "Mick Jackson (director)").

In 2017, Weisz starred in _[My Cousin Rachel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Cousin\_Rachel\_(2017\_film) "My Cousin Rachel (2017 film)")_, a drama based on [Daphne du Maurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daphne_du_Maurier "Daphne du Maurier")'s novel, and in 2018 co-starred in a British [biographical film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biographical_film "Biographical film") about sailor [Donald Crowhurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Crowhurst "Donald Crowhurst"), _[The Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mercy "The Mercy")_, directed by [James Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Marsh_(director) "James Marsh (director)").

Weisz's production company, LC6 Productions, released its first feature film, _[Disobedience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disobedience\_(2017\_film) "Disobedience (2017 film)")_, in 2017, starring Weisz and [Rachel McAdams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_McAdams "Rachel McAdams").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-krollvariety-115)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-turnermm-116) Weisz grew up three [London Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground") stops away from the [Orthodox Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Jewish "Orthodox Jewish") neighborhood where the film is set. Raised within [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism"), Weisz never fully connected to her ancestral religion. She claims she was "really disobedient" herself and has never felt she fits in anywhere.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-117)

In 2018, Weisz played the cutthroat advisor [Lady Sarah Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Churchill,_Duchess_of_Marlborough "Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough") in _[The Favourite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Favourite\_(2018\_film) "The Favourite (2018 film)")_, winning the [BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actress in a Supporting Role")[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-118) and nominated for the [Screen Actors Guild Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_Award_for_Outstanding_Performance_by_a_Cast_in_a_Motion_Picture "Actor Award for Outstanding Performance by a Cast in a Motion Picture"), [Golden Globe Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Actress_in_a_Motion_Picture_%E2%80%93_Drama "Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in a Motion Picture – Drama"), the [Critics' Choice Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critics'_Choice_Movie_Award_for_Best_Actress "Critics' Choice Movie Award for Best Actress"), and the [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-120)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-121)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-122)

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2020s")]

In April 2019, Weisz entered talks to join [Scarlett Johansson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlett_Johansson "Scarlett Johansson") in the [Marvel Cinematic Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Cinematic_Universe "Marvel Cinematic Universe") film _[Black Widow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Widow\_(2021\_film) "Black Widow (2021 film)")_.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-123) In July of that year, Weisz was announced to play [Melina Vostokoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melina_Vostokoff_(Marvel_Cinematic_Universe) "Melina Vostokoff (Marvel Cinematic Universe)") in the film, which was released on 9 July 2021.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-124)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-125)

In 2023, Weisz starred in and executive produced the Prime Video miniseries remake _[Dead Ringers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead\_Ringers\_(miniseries) "Dead Ringers (miniseries)")_, earning a nomination for the Golden Globe Award for Best Actress – Miniseries or Television Film.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-126) She later starred as the lead in the 2026 Netflix limited series _[Vladimir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir\_(TV\_series) "Vladimir (TV series)")_, an adaptation of Julia May Jonas’s novel.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-127) Weisz has been cast in Tomas Alfredson’s upcoming drama _[Séance on a Wet Afternoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A9ance\_on\_a\_Wet\_Afternoon\_(upcoming\_film) "Séance on a Wet Afternoon (upcoming film)")_ opposite Matthew Macfadyen and Joe Alwyn.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-128) She has also been announced to reprise her role as Evelyn O’Connell in the fourth installment of the _[Mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mummy\_(franchise) "The Mummy (franchise)")_ franchise, reuniting with Brendan Fraser and John Hannah; the film is being [developed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmmaking#Development "Filmmaking") by [Radio Silence Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Silence_Productions "Radio Silence Productions") and is scheduled for release in 2028.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-129)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rachel_Weisz&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

In 2001, Weisz began dating filmmaker and producer [Darren Aronofsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darren_Aronofsky "Darren Aronofsky"). They met backstage at London's [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre"), where she was starring in _The Shape of Things_. Weisz moved to New York City with Aronofsky the following year;[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-shape-70) in 2005, they were engaged. Their son was born in May 2006 in New York City.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-usatoday-134)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-135) The couple resided in the [East Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Village,_Manhattan "East Village, Manhattan") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). _Mohel_[Philip Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sherman_(rabbi) "Philip Sherman (rabbi)") performed their son's [brit milah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_milah "Brit milah") ([bris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bris "Bris")).[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-136) In November 2010, Weisz and Aronofsky announced that they had been apart for months but remained close friends and were committed to bringing up their son together in New York.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-peoplesplit-137)

Weisz and the English actor [Daniel Craig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Craig "Daniel Craig") were friends for many years and worked together on the 2011 film _[Dream House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dream\_House\_(2011\_film) "Dream House (2011 film)")_. They began dating in December 2010 and married on 22 June 2011 in a private New York ceremony, with four guests in attendance, including Weisz's son and Craig's daughter.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-138) On 1 September 2018, it was reported that they had their first child together, a daughter, completing their family of 5.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-139)

Weisz has been featured on the covers of magazines such as _[Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogue\_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)")_.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-140) She served as a [muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artistic_inspiration "Artistic inspiration") to the fashion designer [Narciso Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narciso_Rodriguez "Narciso Rodriguez").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-141) Weisz learned [karate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate "Karate") for her role in _[The Brothers Bloom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Brothers\_Bloom "The Brothers Bloom")_.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-142) A British citizen by birth, Weisz became a [naturalised American citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_United_States "Citizenship of the United States") in 2011.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-:0-143)

The database entry of the British Film Institute, citing London birth records gives a year of 1970,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-3) as does the _[Encyclopædia Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A6dia\_Britannica "Encyclopædia Britannica")_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-4) and the National Portrait Gallery.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-5) However, some older sources give it as 1971, including her detailed biography at the [British Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Film_Institute "British Film Institute")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-6) and a biographic article in _The Guardian_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-guardian3-7) The _Evening Standard_ in 2006 claimed that Weisz herself gave 1971 as her year of birth.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz#cite_note-8)

_**The Constant Gardener**_ is a 2005 [drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)")[thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_(genre) "Thriller (genre)") film[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-3) directed by [Fernando Meirelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Meirelles "Fernando Meirelles"). The screenplay by [Jeffrey Caine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Caine "Jeffrey Caine") is based on [John le Carré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_le_Carr%C3%A9 "John le Carré")'s [2001 novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener "The Constant Gardener"). The story follows Justin Quayle ([Ralph Fiennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Fiennes "Ralph Fiennes")), a British diplomat in Kenya, as he tries to solve the murder of his wife Tessa ([Rachel Weisz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Weisz "Rachel Weisz")), an [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") activist, alternating with [flashbacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flashback_(narrative) "Flashback (narrative)") telling the story of their relationship.

The film's title derives from Justin's gentle but diligent attention to his plants throughout the film. The film was a critical and box office success and earned four [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") nominations, winning [Best Supporting Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actress "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress") for Weisz.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Constant_Gardener_(film)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

British diplomat and avid horticulturalist Justin Quayle is confronted by [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") activist Tessa during a lecture in London. They strike up a romance, and marry after she accompanies him to his posting in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"). She befriends Belgian doctor Arnold Bluhm, leading to rumours of an affair. Tessa has no qualms confronting corruption, to the chagrin of Justin's superiors, and she loses a child late in pregnancy.

Tessa and Arnold connect recent local deaths to [drug trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_trial "Clinical trial") being conducted by the Kenyan-based company Three Bees using the drug Dypraxa. They write a damaging report on the drug and Tessa gives it to Justin's colleague Sandy Woodrow, the British [High Commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Commissioner "High Commissioner"), who sends it to Sir Bernard Pellegrin, head of the Africa Desk at the [Foreign Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign,_Commonwealth_and_Development_Office "Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office"). Pellegrin responds with an incriminating letter to Sandy, which Tessa persuades him to show her, and she steals it before departing for [Lokichogio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lokichogio "Lokichogio") with Arnold.

Sandy informs Justin that a white woman and black driver have been killed near [Lake Turkana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Turkana "Lake Turkana"), and that Tessa and Arnold shared a room at [Lodwar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodwar "Lodwar") before hiring a car. Justin and Sandy identify Tessa's mutilated body, but Arnold's whereabouts remain unknown. Police confiscate Tessa's computer and files, but Justin finds her keepsake box, containing a letter from Sandy declaring his love for her and asking her to return Pellegrin's letter, and records of Three Bees' tests.

After Tessa's burial, Justin learns from his colleague Ghita that Tessa kept Arnold's secret that he was gay, as [homosexuality is illegal in Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Kenya "LGBT rights in Kenya"). Pursuing the truth about his wife's murder, he follows the trail of her report. Justin is briefly detained by police and confronts Three Bees' CEO Kenny Curtiss, but receives no answers.

Returning to London, Justin's passport is confiscated. He dines with Pellegrin, who lies that Arnold must have murdered Tessa, and believes that Justin has his incriminating letter. Justin meets with Tessa's cousin and lawyer Ham, and they access her computer files to reveal her investigation into Dypraxa and its manufacturer, [Swiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland")-[Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada")[pharmaceutical conglomerate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_industry "Pharmaceutical industry") KDH, which hired Three Bees to test the drug on unsuspecting Kenyans as a treatment for [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis "Tuberculosis").

Justin receives a threatening note and Ham provides him with a fake passport to travel to Germany to meet with Tessa's contact Birgit. She is part of a pharmaceutical watchdog group and is reluctant to speak due to the targeting of her group. Justin is attacked in his hotel room and warned to stop investigating. Arnold's body is found having been tortured to death, while the announcement of a safe Dypraxa causes KDH's share price to soar.

Returning to Kenya, Justin confronts Sandy, who admits that Tessa's report was silenced to save KDH from spending millions redeveloping the drug. Justin is approached by Curtiss, who has been betrayed by KDH, and brought to a mass grave of Dypraxa test subjects. Curtiss points Justin to Dr Lorbeer, Dypraxa's inventor, who has fled to [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan"). Tim Donohue, a friend in British intelligence, confirms that Pellegrin had Tessa and Arnold killed. Unable to convince Justin to return home, he gives him a gun.

Justin travels to confront Lorbeer, who is treating remote villagers to atone for the lives claimed by his drug. The village is attacked by raiders, but Justin and Lorbeer escape in a [UN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") aid plane, and Lorbeer reveals that he has Pellegrin's letter. Tessa convinced him to record the truth about Dypraxa, but he changed his mind, instead informing KDH that Tessa and Arnold were en route to expose the company to the UN.

Justin convinces the pilot to mail Pellegrin's letter to Ham, and to drop him off at Lake Turkana. Removing the bullets from his gun, his final thoughts are of Tessa before he is killed by KDH's henchmen. In London at Tessa and Justin's memorial service, Pellegrin lies that Justin committed suicide in the same place his wife died.

Ham announces the reading of an [epistle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle "Epistle"), but instead reads Pellegrin's letter, exposing the deaths caused by Dypraxa and the subsequent coverup. Pellegrin storms out as Ham implicates the British government, KDH, and public complacency regarding the human cost of medicine they take for granted.

## Inspiration and themes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Constant_Gardener_(film)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Inspiration and themes")]

The plot of the film is loosely based on a [real-life case in Kano, Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullahi_v._Pfizer,_Inc. "Abdullahi v. Pfizer, Inc.") involving antibacterial testing by Pfizer on small children.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Constant_Gardener_(film)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")]

The film was shot partly in [16mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16mm "16mm")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-4) on location in [Loiyangalani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loiyangalani "Loiyangalani") and the slums of [Kibera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibera "Kibera"), a section of [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"). Circumstances in the area so affected the cast and crew that producer [Simon Channing Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Channing_Williams "Simon Channing Williams") led the creation of the Constant Gardener Trust in order to address issues of sanitation and education in the area.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-7)

Principal photography of the film occurred from May 10, 2004 to August 7, 2004.

[Kate Winslet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Winslet "Kate Winslet") and [Eva Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eva_Green "Eva Green") were considered for the female lead before Weisz was cast.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-8)

[Lupita Nyong'o](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lupita_Nyong'o "Lupita Nyong'o") worked as a production assistant on the film.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-9)

## Reception

### Box office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Constant_Gardener_(film)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Box office")]

The film's worldwide gross was $82,466,670.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-10)

### Critical response

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Constant_Gardener_(film)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Critical response")]

On the film aggregator website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), _The Constant Gardener_ has a score of 83%, based on 192 critical reviews, with an average rating of 7.6/10. The consensus reads, "_The Constant Gardener_ is a smart, gripping, and suspenseful thriller with rich performances from the leads."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-the_constant_gardener-2) It also has a score of 82 out of 100 on [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), based on 39 critics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-11) Audiences polled by [CinemaScore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CinemaScore "CinemaScore") gave the film an average grade of "B" on an A+ to F scale.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-12)

[Roger Ebert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Ebert "Roger Ebert") of the _[Chicago Sun-Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Sun-Times "Chicago Sun-Times")_ called it "one of the year's best films".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-13)_[USA Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA\_Today "USA Today")_ noted that the film's "passion, betrayal, gorgeous cinematography, social commentary, stellar performances and clever wit puts it in a special category near perfection". However, [Michael Atkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Atkinson_(writer) "Michael Atkinson (writer)") of _[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Village\_Voice "The Village Voice")_ criticized the film as "a cannonballing mélange of hack-cuts, impressionistic close-ups, and tropical swelter".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Constant_Gardener_(film)#cite_note-14)

## Author's dedication and afterword

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Constant_Gardener_(film)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Author's dedication and afterword")]

John le Carré, in the first edition of the 2001 novel on which the film is based, provided both a dedication and a personal afterword. The dedication and part of the afterword (amended) are reproduced in the closing credits of the film. The first states: "This film is dedicated to [Yvette Pierpaoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Pierpaoli "Yvette Pierpaoli") and all other aid workers who lived and died giving a damn." The latter continues (in the next credit): "Nobody in this story, and no outfit or corporation, thank God, is based upon an actual person or outfit in the real world. But I can tell you this. As my journey through the pharmaceutical jungle progressed, I came to realize that, by comparison with the reality, my story was as tame as a holiday postcard." The text appears over John le Carré's name.

#### [Beautiful, Haunting and mesmerizing](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0387131/reviews/?featured=rw1162126&ref_=tt_ururv_c_1_hd)

Great romantic thrill ride that is made even more special by the performances of Rachel Weisz and Ralph Fiennes, who both give this adaptation of the John Le Carre book a real sense of beauty, dignity and grace with their on target performances. Weisz is perfection as Tessa Qualye, a civil rights activist who is murdered for trying to bring awareness of their illegal practices on the poor natives of an African village. Weisz gives her character a self-righteous drive that is made poignant by her determination and sheer will and she also makes her character human, not a stereotype, which makes her performance the more real. Ralph Finnes plays her grieving husband Justin, who takes up her cause and begins to lean of how wonderful his wife really was and what he missed during the time she was alive. His haunted performance is in my opinion his best ever and is the driving point of this haunting odyssey of justice, lost and self sacrifice. Rachel Weisz and Ralph Fiennes both deserve Oscar nominations for their superb performances and Fernando Meirelles deserves one as well for his superb direction that puts you smack in the middle of the story that is unfolding right in front of you.  
  
Hands down, the best film of the year so far.

#### [CONSTANCY INEVITABLY UNEARTHS THE TRUTH!](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0387131/reviews/?featured=rw9504417&ref_=tt_ururv_c_2_hd)

The Constant Gardener shines with great intensity, but in a way that is rather subtle, somewhat occult, just beneath the surface.  
  
It's the kind of "Thriller" where more often than not, a silent expression or a nervous pause communicates more than a hundred words of dialogue! Directed with panache, intrigue and passion in both scope and focus by Brazilian Fernando Meirelles (City of God), has created a tale of international dimensions!  
  
Based on the work of John le Carré, Gardener shows us the sinister side of pharmaceutical multinationals, where human life in Third World countries serves to supply their perverse drug trials, in pursuit of ever bigger record profits!  
  
Rachel Weisz (The Mummy, The Mummy Returns, Constantine) has been awarded a much-deserved Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress for her role as activist and wife. Also, Ms. Weisz most certainly deserved her Oscar win! The subtlety, complexity, originality and freshness of her portrayal are nothing short of amazing.  
  
Ralph Fiennes (The English Patient, Maid in Manhattan), despite giving one of the best performances of his life, curiously, did not even receive a Golden Globe nomination!!!  
  
GARDNER demonstrates clearly to us that often the reality of things is not what it seems at first glance.  
  
Justin Quayle (Fiennes) is a mid-level diplomat. He is tormented by persistent rumors and some strong indications of frequent infidelities by his activist wife. When she becomes the victim of a violent and gruesome murder, perhaps at the hands of her alleged African lover, Qualye senses something is askance and begins a methodical and patient investigation. To the extent that he gradually inches closer to the truth, threats and pressures to desist his inquiry increase exponentially!  
  
But as secrets of his late wife's life continue to be revealed, her image has changed completely; Mr. Quayle has become obsessed with arriving at the truth, regardless of the consequences. Also, Quayle, now quite repentant for having doubted his wife to the extent he did, now comes to realize that the most suitable place for him would have been beside the wife who loved him so dearly!.  
  
Thusly, Gardener combines several diverse elements like suspense, political intrigue, romance, action, research and international outreach with masterful skill and powerful intensity.

#### [Not a great movie](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0387131/reviews/?featured=rw1213760&ref_=tt_ururv_c_3_hd)

The constant gardener has it easy. It picks an emotionally charged subject matter and involves issues that are at the forefront of the political agenda. It has to be easier to make a film that has an impact on its audience from this starting point. It could have been genuinely awesome.  
  
However i felt that the film was totally one dimensional. For those that haven't seen it (and this will in no way spoil the plot), the central theme is large biotech companies in Africa. It is undeniable that such companies do exploit the poorer nations but it is likewise undeniable that if such companies didn't exist we would not possess the range of drugs that we do today. There is no question that these companies do some good. With such a rich subject matter an exploration of shades of grey of the debate could be the basis for an excellent film. Sadly the film fell firmly on the anti-biotech side without any sort of fair trial. It is the lack of sophistication about the biotech = bad message that i objected to. Then as if the portrayal wasn't one sided enough anyone involved with either the British government or the biotech company was made a thoroughly unlikeable character in terms of personality.  
  
I don't mean to suggest that as a stand alone piece of work the film was bad. The fact is that by choosing a subject matter that is so emotive the filmmaker must take on certain responsibilities. In the case of the constant gardener i thought the complex issues were not explored at all. We've all seen brilliant movies that balance both sides of a debate, exploring both the "hero's" and the "villain's" motivations, and justifying both to us. The constant gardener does not do this, and i believe is a worse movie for it.

#### [Thought Provoking and Beautifully Stirring Political Potboiler](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0387131/reviews/?featured=rw1166746&ref_=tt_ururv_c_4_hd)

Ralph Fiennes stars as a British diplomat whose complacency is challenged when he is forced into a soul searching quest for the reasons behind the tragic death of his activist wife (Rachel Weisz) that uncovers a sinister pharmaceutical company in cahoots with British and Kenyan governments testing a new TB drug on expendable HIV+ Africans.  
  
Fiennes gives his most humanistic and endearing performance ever, perhaps even topping his Oscar nominated turns in "Schindler's List" and "The English Patient." Rachel Weisz is an illuminating revelation, turning in the performance of her career. Her character develops and becomes even more compelling after she dies and we learn her secrets through expertly paced flashbacks. Director Fernando Meirelles takes the amazing style he honed with "City of God" and adds a heart with "The Constant Gardener," a big heart that bleeds a beautiful cinematic poeticism onto the screen.  
  
This film truly rewards its audience as it works on so many levels. Like this year's earlier word-of-mouth and hot-button issue sleeper, "Crash," you won't be able to stop talking about it after you leave the theater. The politics here are engaging and bound to stir up even the most complacent viewer. What's even more amazing is that all of the timely political discourse and subsequent thriller aspects of the film (courtesy of the source material, John Le Carre's novel) are wrapped up in a timeless romance. We the audience join Fiennes on his journey, and we rediscover the love story between he and his wife that anchors the film in a poetic realism usually reserved for movies with much less on their minds.  
  
To top it off, it's all delivered in the maddeningly genius Meirelles style that took critics and audiences by storm in his debut "City of God". We have the shaky hand-held camera darting through vibrant and colorful third-world locales juxtaposed with jaw-droppingly gorgeous aerial photography of Africa in all its blazing glory. Meirelles again shows us he is a true artist willing to show both the shocking beauty and abject horror of the people and places that populate his films. Again he delivers a message that people are doing horrible things to other people the world over (be it in the form of wishy-washy governments turning a blind eye, greedy corporations putting a price tag on a human life, local thugs preying on the misfortune of their neighbors, or friends betraying friends). With "City of God" he seemed to be saying the only hope is to document it. With "The Constant Gardener" he makes that argument again and takes it one brilliant step forward. We may not be able to stop a war or a huge global injustice, but we do have the power to help one person at a time. It takes a courageous film to make such a statement, and a brilliant film-maker to deliver it, and that's just what "The Constant Gardener" does.

Rachel Weisz brings a ferry fury that is ripe in it's convictions and Ralph Fiennes brings a cool, collective zeal that is a slow building timer ready to emotionally exploded at any minute. Both performances compliment the fine directing of Fernando Meirelles, who gives this tale a sense of brilliance in its storytelling and a sense of the way the world really works. It's a heartfelt story of lost and redemption and it's hauntingly poetic in it's horrifying look at the horrors of a world that is willing to cast a blind eye at the problems of big business and corrupt governments that are willing to do anything in order to make a fast buck. Even going as far than to destroy human life to achieve their goals.  
  
This is a brilliant film and I can't wait to see it again.

Meirelles remembers his first film experiences are related to his father’s movie clips which were shot on 16mm film. However, the career as a director was not Meirelles’s original plan. He grew up in São Paulo and after discontinuing his biology studies Meirelles studied architecture. He decided to become a filmmaker after seeing **Jorge Bodanzky** and **Orlando Senna**’s _Iracema_ (1975). It was a film that combined fiction and documentary such an exceptional way and was so impressive for Meirelles that he decided to make a short film as his final project and, as a result, made his introduction to the film industry. At the beginning of his career, Meirelles and his colleagues made experimental short films and video art. He also directed several years fun and experimental series and worked in advertising. However, the ads were not enough for Meirelles – instead, he dreamed of directing a feature film. He practiced directing a feature film with his first film _Maids_ (2001). “I always want to get involved in projects that make me feel insecure. The topics I don’t know much about and I usually even regret, that I agreed to take on such an impossible idea. For some reason, these work the best in the end.” Meirelles wanted to film **José Saramago**‘s novel _Blindness_, but because of the copyrights, the plan was almost canceled. One of the luckiest coincidences on Meirelles’s career was when the publisher of Saramago asked if Meirelles would be interested in directing **Paulo Lins**‘s novel _The City of God_. After a short moment of hesitation, Meirelles grasped this opportunity and chose a completely different topic. Meirelles’s The City of God was screened at the Cannes Film Festival and was a great success. The film was followed by another success, _The Constant Gardener_ (2005), after which Meirelles announced that he would stop making movies. However, he went back on his decision, as he finally got the opportunity to direct a film adaption of Blindness (2008). The film was followed by _360_ (2011) and then Meirelles returned to TV series. Even after that the director has still broken new ground. Trying something new has always inspired Meirelles. He has directed, for example, the opera _Les Pêcheurs de Perles_ in 2015 and the opening ceremony of the Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro in 2016. Currently, the director has many projects in progress, including a climate crisis series for the BBC, a science documentary and the feature film _The Pope_ produced by Netflix. Meirelles would bring the film Iracema with him to a deserted island.
