_**CZ12**_ ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"):十二生肖; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"):_Shí-èr Shēngxiāo_), also known as _**Armour of God III: Chinese Zodiac**_ and _**Chinese Zodiac**_,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-6) is a 2012 [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film "Action film")[adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_film "Adventure film")[comedy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_film "Comedy film") co-written, co-produced and directed by [Jackie Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan "Jackie Chan"), who also starred as the main character in the film.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-variety-7) A Chinese-Hong Kong co-production, the film is the third film of a franchise that began with _[Armour of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_(film) "Armour of God (film)")_ (1986) and its sequel, _[Armour of God II: Operation Condor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_II:\_Operation\_Condor "Armour of God II: Operation Condor")_ (1991).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-variety-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-hr-review-8) The film co-stars [Kwon Sang-woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwon_Sang-woo "Kwon Sang-woo"), [Liao Fan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_Fan "Liao Fan"), [Zoe Zhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Lanxin "Zhang Lanxin"), [Anna Yao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Yao "Helen Yao") and [Laura Weissbecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Weissbecker "Laura Weissbecker").

The plot follows treasure hunter JC (Chan) and his team who set out on a global quest to find a set of [Chinese zodiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_zodiac "Chinese zodiac") bronze heads that were stolen from a Beijing palace in the 19th century. Released on 20 December 2012, the film went on to gross over US$145 million at the Chinese box office and US$171 million worldwide with mixed-to-negative reviews from critics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-9) The film won Best Stunt Action Choreography for Chan at the [32nd Hong Kong Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Hong_Kong_Film_Awards "32nd Hong Kong Film Awards").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-10) Chan also earned two _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness\_World\_Records "Guinness World Records")_ with the film for "Most Stunts Performed by a Living Actor" and "Most Credits in One Movie".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-TwitchFilm-11)

A sequel, and the fourth film in the _Armour of God_ series, _Armour of God IV: Ultimatum_, is expected to be released in 2027.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-12)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Word representing the position or rank in a sequential order

For the mathematical concept, see [Ordinal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_number "Ordinal number").

Cardinal versus ordinal numbers| Cardinal | one | two | three | four |
| --- |
| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| Ordinal | first | second | third | fourth |
| 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th |

In [linguistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistics "Linguistics"), **ordinal numerals** or **ordinal number words** are words representing position or rank in a [sequential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequential "Sequential") order; the order may be of size, importance, chronology, and so on (e.g., "third", "tertiary"). They differ from [cardinal numerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_numeral "Cardinal numeral"), which represent quantity (e.g., "three") and other types of numerals.

## Grammar

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ordinal_numeral&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Grammar")]

In traditional grammar, all [numerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numeral_(linguistics) "Numeral (linguistics)"), including ordinal numerals, are grouped into a separate [part of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Part_of_speech "Part of speech") ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _nomen numerale_, hence, "noun numeral" in older English grammar books). However, in modern interpretations of [English grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_grammar "English grammar"), ordinal numerals are usually considered [adjectives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjective "Adjective").

Ordinal numbers may be written in English with numerals and letter suffixes: 1st, 2nd or 2d, 3rd or 3d, 4th, 11th, 21st, 101st, 477th, etc., with the suffix acting as an [ordinal indicator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_indicator "Ordinal indicator"). Written dates often omit the suffix, although it is nevertheless pronounced. For example: 5 November 1605 (pronounced "the fifth of November ... "); November 5, 1605, ("November (the) Fifth ..."). When written out in full with "of", however, the suffix is retained: the 5th of November. In other languages, different ordinal indicators are used to write ordinal numbers.

## How ordinals are formed by language

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ordinal_numeral&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: How ordinals are formed by language")]

### Oral/spoken languages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ordinal_numeral&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Oral/spoken languages")]

#### English

Look up _**[Appendix:English ordinal numbers](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Appendix:English%20ordinal%20numbers "wiktionary:Appendix:English ordinal numbers")**_ in Wiktionary, the free dictionary.

In English, the main ordinal series is 'first', 'second', .... It is used in a variety of rankings, including time ('the first hour of the event'), space ('the first left'), and quality ('first class cabin').

With the exception of the word 'second', the main ordinal series are all words derived from Old English.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] ('Second', which came from Latin into English via French around 1300, replaced the Old English word for 'other', which no longer carries the definition of second, except in certain phrases like "every other day").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

# 7-Day Kungfu Experience – One Week

## Chinese Kungfu Experience

## Suggested Itinerary

Day 1 Arrive in Zhengzhou, Transfer to Dengfeng

A guide will meet you at the arrivals of Zhengzhou Airport and take you in a private car to Dengfeng, where you will attend the Kungfu School Entrance Ceremony, and settle in the school hotel.Your tour guide will accompany you the whole tour.

Day 2 Songyang Academy, Songyue Temple and Shaolin Temple

The ancient Songyang Academy at the foot of Taishi Mountain north of Dengsheng was one of the four Tang Dynasty academie. Zhongyue Temple was rebuilt in Qing Dynasty and looks remarkably like the Forbidden City.

Shaolin Temple, the birthplace of Wushu, is famous from the ancient legends. Monks display their skills in a small theater several times a day. Pagoda Forest nearby has a multitude of miniature brick pagodas built over centuries, each honoring a particular kungfu master.

Lunch in the Yongtai Nunnery includes only vegetarian dishes, but in the evening a Chinese dinner is available in the village.

Good to Know:

Zen Music Shaolin Grand Ceremony is an extraordinary outdoor show, where hundreds of monks together with village people perform aerial sword fights and synchronized fight formations woven into a story against a backdrop of mountains and water. Ask your travel advisor to book tickets for you if you are interested.

Day 3 - 6 Training Course

You will learn kungfu in the following three days. On this first day of the core training course you must select an area to concentrate on: Step Boxing, Baduanjin, Yijinjing, Xiao Hong Quan or Qigong. One or two other subjects can be chosen as optional extras.

Day 7 Kungfu School Farewell Ceremony, Depart Dengfeng, Transfer to Zhengfeng

After the farewell ceremony at the Kungfu School, your tour guide and driver escort you from Dengfeng to Zhengzhou Airport for your departure flight.

# Best Time to Visit China: Avoid the Crowds (Travel Calendar)

To be honest, we think the best time to travel to China is almost all year round. Because China is a large country and you can always find a suitable destination every month.

This article will help you choose the best time to visit most cities, show you how to match destinations with your travel month, and share useful weather [tips for each season](https://www.chinahighlights.com/weather/china-best-times.htm#month).

## When Is China at Its Best?

### Autumn Is Best, Spring Comes Second

Spring (March-May) and autumn (September-November) are the best times to enjoy pleasant weather and beautiful natural scenery.

**Autumn**, in particular, is ideal for most cities across China. There's little rain, the summer heat fades, and outdoor sightseeing becomes much more comfortable.

The landscapes come alive with color like the blue lakes of Jiuzhaigou, red maple leaves in Beijing's Xiangshan Park, and golden ginkgo trees at the Forbidden City.

**It's a great season for** nature lovers, photographers, and anyone who enjoys being outdoors.

Check out our [14-Day Beijing–Xi'an–Zhangjiajie–Guilin–Shanghai](https://www.chinahighlights.com/china-tours/natural-wonders-discovery.htm)

![Image 29: Best month to visit China](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Shuzheng Lakes in Jiuzhaigou (autumn views)

**Spring** is just as beautiful as autumn, especially with all the **blooming flowers**.

You can see vibrant rapeseed fields in Luoping and Huangshan, jacaranda trees in Kunming, and peach blossoms in Tibet.

However, spring tends to have slightly more rain, particularly in southern cities like Guilin, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, but it's usually light and won't affect your travel too much.

![Image 30: Best month to visit China](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Vibrant rapeseed fields in Luoping, Yunnan

**Inside Tips: Avoid Peak Holiday Crowds**

During spring and autumn, we recommend avoiding the following dates. These are major public holidays in China, when tourist sites are extremely crowded and travel costs can rise by 50–100%:

*   Qingming Festival (April 3–5)
*   Labor Day (April 30 – May 4)
*   National Day (September 30 – October 6)

So, taking crowds, weather, and scenery into account, the best months to travel are April, May, September, and mid-to-late October.

If you're heading to southern destinations like Yunnan or Guilin, early November is also a great option.

See more travel tips on [Dates You Should Avoid When Planning a China Tour](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/article/avoiding-travel-dates.htm)

[![Image 31: Best month to visit China](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)](https://www.chinahighlights.com/china-tours/classic-tour.htm)

[**12-Day Tour: Beijing – Xi'an – Guilin/Yangshuo – Shanghai**Classic Wonders](https://www.chinahighlights.com/china-tours/classic-tour.htm)

[](https://www.chinahighlights.com/china-tours/classic-tour.htm)

### What If I Can Only Travel in Summer or Winter?

While not everyone can travel in spring or autumn, especially if you're planning a family trip during your children's winter or summer holidays.

**Summer** is one of the most popular travel times for Chinese families. Thus,**it is the peak season**. But with the right planning and local insights, you could still enjoy a comfortable and enriching trip.

**How to Beat Summer Crowds:**

**1. Choose the right route or section, not just the attraction.**

Most major sights have more than one way to explore them, and some are far less crowded. For example:

*   [The Great Wall](https://www.chinahighlights.com/greatwall/how-to-visit.htm): [Jinshanling](https://www.chinahighlights.com/greatwall/section/jinshanling-greatwall.htm) and [Jiankou](https://www.chinahighlights.com/greatwall/section/jiankou-greatwall.htm) sections see far fewer tourists than the famous Badaling.
*   [Terracotta Warriors](https://www.chinahighlights.com/xian/terracotta-army/how-to-visit.htm): Start with Pit 3 (the quietest), then visit Pit 2, and finish with Pit 1, going against the typical flow.
*   [Forbidden City](https://www.chinahighlights.com/beijing/forbidden-city/how-to-visit.htm): Begin with the side halls instead of the main central axis to avoid the early rush.

**2. Go early or late to avoid peak times.**

Most tourist hotspots are **busiest between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m**.

# China Weather in January 2026: A Good Time to Visit?

**If you love snowy scenery or prefer to travel when it's quieter and more affordable, January is a great time to visit.**

January is the coldest month in China. Large parts of China reach the peak of severe winter weather except for locations in South China, such as Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Macau, and Hainan Island. These places are comfortable winter escapes for people from colder latitudes.

Snow falls in North China (in areas such as Harbin and Beijing). If you want to enjoy stunning snow scenery and exciting snow activities, go to North China.

Read on to get more China in January weather information and our useful travel tips.

![Image 29: Chengdu Bipenggou Valley](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)

## Top 5 Places to Visit in China in January

Here are 5 popular winter destinations in January in China where you could enjoy a wonderful winter holiday with everything from beautiful snowy scenery to vibrant cultural experiences.

### 1. Yunnan: Where Snow Meets Sunshine

![Image 30: Chengdu Bipenggou Valley](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Jade Dragon Snow Mountain

Ranging from tropical rainforests to snow-capped peaks, [Yunnan in January](https://www.chinahighlights.com/yunnan/weather-in-january.htm) would give you more options in winter.

In Kunming, Lijiang, and Shangri-La, you can marvel at the snow-covered **Jiaozi**, **Jade Dragon**, and **Meili Snow Mountains** — January is one of the best times of the year to enjoy their breathtaking alpine views.

In Dali, Kunming, and Lijiang, the city areas stay comfortably warm in winter. It is perfect for outdoor sightseeing.

You could ride a **bike along Erhai Lake**, take a relaxing walk through Lijiang Ancient Town, or **visit a local farm** with your kids to make the region's famous flower cakes as a special New Year's treat.

If you're looking to escape the cold and experience somewhere even warmer, head south to Xishuangbanna. There, you could go on an adventure in the tropical rainforest, explore Dai villages and their local cuisine, or unwind in the nearby [Jingmai Mountain](https://www.chinahighlights.com/xishuangbanna/attraction/jingmai-mountain.htm), surrounded by tea plantations and forest trails.

### 2. Harbin & Jilin: Best Place for Snow Activities

![Image 31: Chengdu Bipenggou Valley](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Ice and Snow World

If you want to see the snow and participate in a variety of snow and ice activities, then Harbin is the place for you.

The annual [Harbin Ice and Snow Festival](https://www.chinahighlights.com/festivals/harbin-ice-and-snow-festival.htm) is open and offers a mesmerising winter wonderland. Marvel at the intricate ice sculptures, ice castles, and even enjoy thrilling ice slides.

If you like photography and look for spectacular winter scenery, the rime wonder of Jilin City should not be missed. The best spots to see the rime ice are the Ashhada Rime Ice Viewing Belt and Rime Ice Island.

You could also go to **China Snow Town** to feel the magic of seeing splashed water instantly turn into ice and experience the traditional winter lifestyle in northeast China, such as staying on a traditional _kang bed_ (a brick bed heated by a fire underneath) and making dumplings.

### 3. Beijing: Enjoy the Less-Crowded Great Wall

![Image 32: Chengdu Bipenggou Valley](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Our clients visiting the Great Wall in winter

Beijing remains a popular choice for first-time visitors to China, regardless of the season.

January is the **off-season** in Beijing. You could enjoy better prices. Attractions are less crowded, so you could spend more time exploring rather than waiting in line.

In January, you have the opportunity to witness the breathtaking **snow-covered scenery** of the Great Wall. This dry and cold season also allows for hiking, and you could enjoy a less-crowded experience on the Great Wall.

Beijing also offers great opportunities for skiing in winter. You could enjoy the fun at an Olympic resort and skate with locals on a frozen lake.

Furthermore, you could experience vibrant celebrations at the **Chinese New Year**, which typically occurs at the end of January or in the beginning/middle of February.

# History of China: Timeline Summary, Dynasties of China, Maps

China is one of the world's **four ancient civilizations**, and the written history of China dates back to the Shang Dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BC), over 3,000 years ago.

## Timeline of Chinese History

| Year | Era | Dynasty | Capital | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2100–1600 BC | Ancient China | Xia | Luoyang Dengfeng Zhengzhou | The first dynasty in traditional Chinese historiography |
| 1600–1046 BC | Shang | Anyang | First dynasty to have historical records remaining |
| 1046–221 BC | Zhou | Xi'an Luoyang | Confucianism emerged |
| 221–206 BC | Imperial China | Qin | Xi'an | First to unite China as a country under an emperor |
| 206 BC – 220 AD | Han | Xi'an Luoyang | The same period as the Roman Empire |
| 220–581 | Wei, Jin, Northern and Southern Dynasties | Luoyang Chengdu Nanjing | Frequent regime changes |
| 581–618 | Sui | Xi'an Luoyang | A system was established to select talents by examination |
| 618–907 | Tang | Xi'an Luoyang | It had the only female emperor. |
| 960–1279 | Song | Kaifeng Hangzhou | Printing, the compass, and gunpowder were invented. |
| 1271–1368 | Yuan | Beijing | The first foreign regime to unite China |
| 1368–1644 | Ming | Nanjing Beijing | Most of the Great Wall today was built or repaired during the Ming Dynasty. |
| 1644–1912 | Qing | Beijing | The last dynasty of China |
| 1912–1949 | Republic of China | Republic of China | Beijing Wuhan Nanjing |  |
| 1949–present | Modern China | People's Republic of China | Beijing |  |

A more detailed table please see [China's historical timeline](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/china-history/timeline.htm) and some key events. There's also a simple comparison with the world's historical development.

[![Image 29: Map of Qing Dynasty](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Click to enlarge!](https://images.chinahighlights.com/allpicture/2017/07/99a04d09f69f4ac7b474c509.jpg)

## Dynasties of China in Order

Before the emergence of the dynasties, China was a [primitive society](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/china-history/prehistoric-time.htm).

Some of the **earliest human remains** were found in China: Yuanmou Man, found in Yunnan, Lantian Man in Shaanxi Province, and Peking Man.

**Peking Man** could use fire and made stone implements. They lived in groups as hunter-gatherers. This was the first stage of primitive society.

**17,000 years ago**, evidence suggests Upper Cave Man formed a relatively fixed group of blood relations. Such clans also appeared in Banpo Village in Xi'an and other archeological sites along the Yangtze River. Then people farmed and raised animals. This is the second stage of primitive.

From the clans, dynasties coalesced.

### The Xia Dynasty (2070–1600 BC)

*   [The Xia Dynasty](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/china-history/the-xia-dynasty.htm) was considered as the **first dynasty** of ancient China.
*   It's generally believed that the Xia Dynasty consisted of several clans **living alongside the Yellow River**.
*   The Xia Dynasty is traditionally considered to be the **beginning of China's hereditary dynasty**.
*   **Considered mythical** by many historians, Xia era relics found in a site called Erlitou in the central Yellow River Basin are yet to be conclusively linked with the Xia Dynasty as described in Zhou Dynasty writings.

### The Shang Dynasty (1600–1046 BC)

![Image 30: Map of Qing Dynasty](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Map of Shang Dynasty

*   [The Shang Dynasty](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/china-history/the-shang-dynasty.htm) was the first dynasty with **historical records** remaining.
*   The **earliest form of Chinese writing** — oracle bones — were found to tally with later accounts of the Shang Dynasty.
*   **Chinese civilization** truly began along the Yellow River in the Shang era.
*   The Simuwu Rectangular Ding in the National Museum of China was made in the Shang Dynasty is the **largest bronze vessel** ever found in the world.

### The Zhou Dynasty (1045-221 BC)

![Image 31: Map of Qing Dynasty](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)Map of Western Zhou

*   The Zhou Dynasty was divided into the Western Zhou (1045–771 BC), the [Spring and Autumn Period](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/china-history/spring-and-autumn-period.htm) (770–476 BC), and [the Warring States Period](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/china-history/warring-states-period.htm) (475–221 BC). The latter periods are also known as the Eastern Zhou.
*   Compared with the peace and prosperity of the Western Zhou, the Eastern Zhou was a period of great division. The Zhou king lost his authority and **seven prominent states emerged**.

# Lucky Numbers and Unlucky Numbers in China

In China, lucky numbers have pronunciations that are similar to words with lucky meanings. **Number 8 holds huge significance as a lucky number**. To a lesser extent 2, 6, and 9 are considered lucky. **4 is the most unlucky number in China**. As well as these general number superstitions, _fengshui_ and the Chinese zodiac dictate different number luck for different places/people.

## Content Preview

*   [Chinese Numbers Combinations and Their Meanings](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/culture/lucky-number-8.htm#combination)
*   [The Chinese Zodiac Lucky/Unlucky Numbers](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/culture/lucky-number-8.htm#zodiac)

## The Lucky Numbers in China

In Chinese culture, people believe that lucky numbers can bring them good luck and fortune. So, it is important for Chinese people to choose a good number for important items, such as wedding dates, dates of moving into a new house, numbers of car license plates, telephone numbers, and so on.

The numbers 8, 2, 6, and 9 are the favorite lucky numbers of most Chinese people. Combinations of the above are deemed as lucky numbers too, such as 66, 88, 168.

### Number 8 — the Luckiest Number in China

The number 8 is believed to be the luckiest number in China because '8' is associated with wealth. 'Eight' (八) in Chinese is pronounced ba and sounds similar to fa (发, traditional character: 發) as in facai (发财), meaning 'well-off' or 'becoming rich in a short time'.

![Image 29: unlucky numbers in China](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)The Number 8

There are many phrases or expressions associated with '8', such as "Bamian laicai" (八面来財 — '8 sides coming wealth'), which means 'wealth coming in from all corners of the world' and "Bamian chunfeng" (八面春风 — '8 sides spring wind'), meaning 'spring wind from eight directions', expressing the wish that someone gets luck wherever s/he goes, or whatever s/he is working on.

Chinese people would like to choose '8' as the time and/or date of important events. For example, the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympic Games commenced exactly at 8 minutes and 8 seconds past 8 pm on the 8th of August 2008.

Chinese' fondness for 8 can be seen in many other cases, such as house numbers, phone numbers, number plates, wedding dates, the date for opening a business, and so on. 8 is considered lucky and favored by Chinese because it holds meaning in both traditional and modern cultures.

### The Number 6

6 (六), pronounced _liu,_ is considered lucky as it sounds like the word that means 'to flow', and can indicate smooth progress in life. It also means well-off. Similar to 8, 6 is preferred in number plates and phone numbers. When a couple gets engaged, the man customarily offers a gift to the girl's family which is usually money (RMB 6,666 and such) and this gift signifies a harmonious life for the couple.

If a person is to celebrate their 66th birthday, that is a grand occasion. In business, 6 is considered lucky. New ventures or contracts are signed on dates that have 6 in them.

### The Number 9

9 (久), pronounced _jiu_, is a popular number, much like 6 and 8. It is similar to the word that means everlasting. It is common to gift your beloved 99 roses on Valentine's Day in China. 9 is the highest single digit number and hence represents completeness.

This made it very popular with Emperors who used it in many aspects of their administration, right from dividing the empire into 9 continents, wearing nine-dragon imperial robes, nine-rank system for officials, etc. In Chinese mythology, it is said that the Dragon has 9 children.

### The Number 2

![Image 30: unlucky numbers in China](https://data.chinahighlights.com/grey.gif)The Number 2

Chinese strongly believe in harmony and balance, hence even numbers naturally gain preference over odd numbers. The number 0 is a whole number as well as an even one, especially for money, and is thus considered a lucky digit.

# Chinese Names

[](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/guidebook/chinese-names.htm)

In Chinese culture, name plays an important role in Chinese people's life. Parents have a great responsibility to choose a good name for their baby. Chinese parents believe good names will bring good luck and fortune to their child.

## Content Preview

*   [How to Choose Your Chinese Name](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/guidebook/chinese-names.htm#how)

## Chinese Names: Surname + Given Name

Chinese names consist of a family name and a given name. The family name comes first followed by a given name. Most family names are just one Chinese character. A few have two characters. Most given names have two characters, some have one, and very occasionally three are used.

### Top 10 Most Common Chinese Surnames

Chinese "surnames" (family name) come first when written, opposite to the Western name order. There are about 2,000 Chinese surnames in use today, but about half of all Han Chinese people share the same 19 surnames!

The most common surnames are Wang and Li (each with about 7% of China's population, compared to about 0.8% for Smith, the USA's most common surname). The next 8 in the top 10 most common Chinese surnames are: Zhang, Liu, Chen, Yang, Huang, Zhao, Wu, and Zhou.

**Changing Your Name After Marriage?**In China, women don't change their surnames when they get married. And nowadays, kids' surnames can be the same as their mother's or father's (or they could take both, like a double-barreled surname). Traditionally, Chinese children always take their father's family name.

### Chinese Given Names

Almost all Chinese given names are made up of one, two, or three Chinese characters, which are written after the surnames. Two-character given names are by far the most popular for most Chinese.

# Chinese Zodiac

 The Chinese zodiac, also known as Shengxiao, is a traditional Chinese system that uses 12 animals to mark the years and calculate age. Specifically, the 12 animals - Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Sheep, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, and Pig - cycle in a fixed order, with each year corresponding to one animal. The animal corresponding to a person’s year of birth is their zodiac animal sign. The Chinese zodiac also carries rich cultural connotations, including personality analysis, fortune-telling, and marriage compatibility guidance, similar to Western astrology.  
  
2026 is the [year of the Horse](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/intro/social_customs/zodiac/horse.htm) according to the Chinese zodiac, symbolizing passion, drive, and vitality. It starts from February 17, 2026, the day of the [Chinese New Year](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/chinese-new-year.htm), and ends on February 5, 2027. Those born during this period are of the Horse zodiac sign and are generally characterized by an outgoing, independent, and freedom-loving personality.  

## Origin of the Chinese Zodiac

Why are these 12 animals selected as the Chinese zodiac? Legend has it that a long time ago, the Jade Emperor, the supreme ruler who presides over the three realms of heaven, earth, and humanity in Chinese mythology, wanted to find a simple way to mark the years in the mortal world, so he decided to choose twelve animals to serve as the “Zodiac Ambassadors.” He proclaimed to the world: on the first day of the first lunar month, the animals were to compete in a river-crossing race, and the first twelve to reach the finish line would become the twelve zodiac animal signs.  
  
The honest Ox swam the fastest, but the clever Rat had been hiding on its back the whole time. Just before the finish line, the Rat leaped down and snatched first place, leaving the Ox to settle for second. The Tiger, relying on its brute strength and speed, swam vigorously to the other side and claimed third place. # Chinese New Year 2026

![Image 2: Chinese New Year](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2010/spring-festival.jpg)

| Chinese: | 春节 chūn jié |
| --- |
| Also called: | Lunar New Year, Spring Festival |
| Observed by: | All Chinese people; people in some other Asian countries like Malaysia, Singapore, Philippines… |
| 2026 date: | Tuesday, Feb. 17th, Horse |
| 2027 date: | Saturday, Feb. 6th, Sheep |
| Holiday: | 9 days |

## China's Grandest Festival & Longest Public Holiday

**2026 Chinese New Year date: Feb. 17th, Tuesday, Year of the Horse**

Chinese New Year, also known as Spring Festival or Lunar New Year, is the grandest festival in China, usually with a 9 days'holiday. As the most colorful annual event, the traditional CNY celebration lasts longer, up to two weeks, and the climax arrives around the Lunar New Year's Eve.  
  
China during this period is dominated by iconic red lanterns, loud fireworks, massive banquets and parades, and the festival even triggers exuberant celebrations across the globe.

## 2026 – [The Year of the Horse](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/intro/social_customs/zodiac/horse.htm)

In 2026 Chinese New Year festival falls on Feb. 17th. It is the Year of the Horse according to the Chinese zodiac, which features a 12-year cycle with each year represented by a specific animal. People born in the Years of the Horse including 1930, 1942, 1954, 1966, 1978, 1990, and 2026 will experience their Zodiac Year of Birth (Ben Ming Nian). 2027 Chinese New Year falls on Feb. 6th and it is the [Year of Sheep](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/intro/social_customs/zodiac/sheep.htm).  

## Time for Family Reunion

Like Christmas in Western countries, Chinese New Year is a time to be home with family, chatting, drinking, cooking, and enjoying a hearty meal together.  
  
![Image 3](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)[10 Facts You Should Know about Chinese New Year](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/facts.htm)

![Image 4: Horse Lantern in the Horse Year](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2026/horse-lantern-festival.jpg)
2026, the Year of Horse

![Image 5: 2028 Chinese New Year Calendar](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2023/1023091023.jpg)

2026

2027

2028

## When is Chinese New Year?

Unlike the universal New Year observed on January 1st, Chinese New Year is never on a fixed date. The dates vary according to Chinese lunar calendar, but generally fall on a day between January 21st and February 20th in the Gregorian calendar.  

How long is the festival? Most people in China have at least seven days off work, including three days' legal holiday, and the preceding and following weekends. Here's a CNY timetable for recent years, marked in UTC/GMT+08:00.  

![Image 6](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)[Chinese New Year 2026: Dates & Calendar](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/dates.htm)  

| Year | Date | Day | Holiday |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026 | Feb.17 | Tuesday | Feb.15 - Feb. 23 |
| 2027 | Feb.6 | Saturday | Feb. 4 - Feb.12 |
| 2028 | Jan. 26 | Wednesday | Jan. 24 - Feb. 1 |

| 2030 | Feb. 3 | Sunday | Feb. 1 - 9 |

## Why is it called Spring Festival?

The festival date is in January or February, around the Chinese solar term the 'Beginning of Spring', so it is also named the 'Spring Festival'.  
  

## [How do Chinese people celebrate the festival?](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/celebration.htm) – Customs & Activities

When all streets and lanes are decorated with vibrant red lanterns and colorful lights, the Lunar New Year is approaching. What do Chinese people do then? After half a month's busy time with a house spring-clean and holiday shopping, the festivities kick off on the New Year's Eve, and last 15 days, until the full moon arrives with the Lantern Festival. Scroll down and let's look through the core traditions and practices of the Chinese New Year.
![Image 7: Shopping for Chinese New Year](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2012/1219155139.jpg) Shopping for Chinese New Year![Image 8: Lantern Festival](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2018/1026154831.jpg) Lantern Festival
  

### House Cleaning and Decorating – half month before

![Image 9: Spring Festival Couplets](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2026/spring-festival-couplet.jpg)
Spring Festival Couplets
No matter whether in a city apartment or a countryside villa, there must be a diligent housewife exerting all her energies to carry out a thorough clean of the house before Chinese New Year. Sweeping, mopping, wiping, washing… Sometimes the whole family needs to give a hand with the chores, to make sure the house is rid of the old year's dust and is prepared for taking in the fortune of the New Year. Then every house is decorated with the most favored color, the bright Red – [red lanterns](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/lantern/), Chinese knots, [Spring Festival couplets](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/spring-festival-couplets.htm), 'Fu'character pictures, and red window [paper-cuts](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/intro/arts/paper_cut.htm).Read more about [How to Decorate for Chinese New Year](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/decorations.htm).

### Family Reunion Dinner – New Year's Eve

![Image 10: Family Reunion](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2018/1026153839.jpg)
Family Reunion
Home is the principal focus of the Spring Festival. All Chinese people manage to make their way home at the latest by New Year's Eve, for a reunion dinner with the whole family. The essential course on all Chinese menus for a reunion dinner will be a steamed or braised whole fish, representing a surplus every year. Various kinds of meat, vegetable, and seafood are made into dishes with auspicious meanings. Dumplings are indispensable for northerners, while rice cakes for southerners. The night is spent enjoying this feast along with cheerful family talk and laughter. Read more [Chinese New Year Foods](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/food.htm).

### Giving Red Envelopes – Best Wishes through Money

![Image 11: Red Envelopes](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2017/red-envelope.jpg)
Red Envelopes
From newborn babies to teenagers, luck money will be given by seniors, wrapped in red packets in the hope of dispelling evil spirits from the kids. CNY 100 to 500 notes are commonly sealed in a red envelope, while there are big ones with up to CNY 5,000 especially in the rich southeast regions. Besides a small disposable amount, most of the money is used to buy the kids toys, snacks, clothes, stationery, or saved for their future educational expenditure. Read more about [Red Envelope](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/red-envelope.htm).

### Send Greetings and Red Envelopes through Wechat

With the popularity of instant messaging apps, greeting cards are seldom seen. From the morning to the midnight of the New Year's Eve, people use the app Wechat to send various text messages, voice messages, and emojis, some of which featuring the New Year's animal sign, to exchange greetings and good wishes. Digital red envelopes are becoming considerably popular and a big red envelope in a group chat always starts a happy grabbing game.

### Watching CCTV New Year's Gala – 20:00 to 00:30

It is undeniable that the [CCTV New Year's Gala](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/gala.htm) is China's most watched television special, despite the declining viewership in recent years. The 4.5-hour live broadcast features music, dance, comedy, opera, and acrobatic performances. Although the audience becomes more and more critical of the programs, that never stops people turning on the TV on time. The delightful songs and words act as a habitual background to a reunion dinner, for after all it's been a tradition ever since 1983.

### Setting off Firecrackers at 00:00

There is New Year bell on the TV gala at 0:00, but you can hardly hear it since there would be loud bangs of [firecrackers](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/firework.htm), from 0:00 to 0:30 and even later. Chinese people have by long tradition set off firecrackers, originally to scare away the legendary monster Nian which emerges at midnight. In recent years, many urban areas have a firecracker ban or set special area or period for fireworks, to prevent accidents and threats to air quality.

![Image 12: Firecrackers](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/images/photogallery/2018/1123113029.jpg)
Firecrackers

### Half-month Visiting Relatives – from One Family to Another

After a day at home, people start to visit relatives from the second day of the New Year. The married couples go to visit the wife's parents'home on the second day. The following days will be spent in various relatives'houses. For some extended families in rural areas, half a month is barely enough to visit everyone. People bring gifts to one another's homes and give red envelopes to the kids. That's a ritual. Get inspired by more [Chinese New Year Gift Ideas](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/essential/holidays/new-year/gifts-ideas.htm).

### Folk Shows and Temple Fairs – Lasting to 15th day of 1st lunar month

In urban areas, there are bustling temple fairs with religious worship, costume performances, games, and local snacks. Some locations have lantern fairs, offering great night fun. In rural areas, more authentic folk shows are likely to be seen, including the yangko dance and stilt walking in north China and dragon and lion dances prevailing in southern regions. See [Best Temple Fairs in Beijing](https://www.travelchinaguide.com/cityguides/beijing/temple-fairs.htm).

# Year of the Rooster

 The Rooster ranks the tenth among the 12 Chinese zodiac signs. Recent Rooster years include 1933, 1945, 1957, 1969, 1981, 1993, 2005 and 2017, and the next Rooster year will be 2029.  
  
The rooster crows faithfully at dawn every day, projecting an air of diligence, self-discipline, shrewdness, and capability. Such traits can also be commonly seen in those born in the Year of the Rooster. In 2026, Rooster persons will enjoy generally stable fortune with no major calamities. Though they may encounter minor setbacks and pressure, this year is ideal for accumulating strength for growth and achieving personal self-improvement.  

## How did Rooster Become a Chinese Zodiac Sign?

In ancient China, people equally divided the day into 12 time periods. The tenth period runs from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. - exactly the time when farmers finished their daily work and called their roosters back to the henhouse. As time went by, this period became closely associated with the rooster. Consequently, the rooster claimed its place as the tenth animal in the Chinese zodiac.  
  
Furthermore, the rooster is an auspicious symbol in Chinese culture, because its pronunciation is nearly the same with the Chinese character “吉” that stands for auspiciousness. Symbolizing blessings and good fortune, this serves as another key reason why the rooster was chosen as one of the 12 zodiac animals.  
  
However, you may be more interested in its mythological origin instead. Long ago, the Jade Emperor, supreme ruler of all, decided to select 12 animals that contributed the most to humans to form the Chinese zodiac. The Rooster rushed eagerly to sign up, but being eliminated in the first round. The judges pointed out that it was quarrelsome by nature. Besides, as a bird, it did not qualify as a candidate land animal. Seeing the Horse, Ox, Dog, and other animals being selected effortlessly, the Rooster was filled with envy and disappointment.  
  
The Rooster later turned to the already chosen Horse and asked how it could get a second chance. “Dedicate yourself to serving people with genuine deeds and earn their sincere respect,” the Horse replied. The Rooster sank into deep contemplation, wondering what meaningful things it could do for mankind.  
  
Early the next morning, the Rooster was roused by a sudden stir of chaos. The farmers had overslept and were hurrying frantically off to their fields. A brilliant thought suddenly struck the Rooster: it possessed a loud, resonant crow and could wake all the villagers up at a fixed time every day. At first, the Rooster struggled to get the timing right. It crowed in the dead of night, waking the entire village and earning a scolding from everyone. Undeterred, it kept a close watch on the sunrise each day, and in time, perfected the skill of crowing precisely at dawn. From that day onward, the farmers never missed their farming duties again.  
  
The villagers were full of gratitude toward the Rooster and jointly pleaded with the Jade Emperor to grant it a place in the Chinese zodiac. Even so, the Jade Emperor stood firmly by his rule of selecting only land-dwelling animals. Overwhelmed with grief, the Rooster wept day and night. One night, the Jade Emperor dreamed of this hardworking Rooster and was deeply touched by its perseverance. He plucked a red flower from the front of his palace hall and gently set it atop the Rooster’s head.  
  
When the Rooster woke up the next morning, it was overjoyed to find the imperial red flower indeed resting on its head. The Four Heavenly Kings - four mighty divine guardians - saw this and understood the Jade Emperor’s unspoken will. They made a special exception and allowed the Rooster to join the final zodiac selection race.  
  
On the day of the contest, the Rooster rushed toward the Heavenly Court, the sacred abode where all gods dwell, arriving almost at the same time with the Dog. At the decisive moment, the Rooster spread its wings and darted forward, crossing the threshold a split second ahead. That is how it claimed its place as the tenth animal in the Chinese zodiac.  

## Years of the Rooster

The Chinese zodiac follows a 12-year cycle. Notably, the yearly shift does not occur on January 1st of the Gregorian calendar; instead, the accurate day of shift is Chinese New Year, which typically arrives between late January and mid-February. For example, Chinese New Year in 2017 fell on January 28th. The days before this date belongs to the previous Year of the Monkey, while only those born on and after the day have the Rooster sign. ## Lucky / Unlucky Signs for People Born in Rooster Year

In Western astrology, every star sign is ruled by one of the four fundamental elements: Earth, Air, Fire and Water. The Chinese zodiac follows a similar pattern, with each sign bound to one or several China’s traditional Five Elements - Metal, Wood, Water, Fire and Earth. The Rooster zodiac sign is affiliated with the Metal. All lucky and inauspicious symbols for Rooster people are judged by a core standard: whether they amplify or weaken the inherent energy of Metal. In a simple logic, Water and Earth strengthen Metal’s energy, while Wood and Fire weaken it. As a practical example, Earth-related tones such as yellow and brown bring good fortune to Rooster persons. Conversely, red - a color aligned with the Fire - tends to exert an adverse impact on their overall luck.  

### Lucky and Unlucky Numbers

Lucky numbers: 5,7,8  
Unlucky numbers: 1,3,9  
Recommendations: When selecting phone numbers, residential floors, and vehicle license plates, prioritize the numbers 5, 7 and 8 and their various combinations. Arrange important meetings, contract signings and trips on dates that feature these auspicious numbers whenever possible. By contrast, it is best to avoid 1, 3 and 9 in daily life. Refrain from arranging major life events or large investments on dates associated with these digits.  

### Lucky and Unlucky Colors

Lucky colors: gold, brown, yellow  
Unlucky colors: green, red  
Recommendations: Opt for gold, brown and yellow more often in daily outfits, personal accessories, and home decor to boost fortune. When dressing for important occasions, steer clear of green and red to minimize any unfavorable impact.  

### Lucky Flowers

Gladiolas, impatiens, and cockscombs are the auspicious flowers for those born in the Year of the Rooster. Cockscombs align perfectly with the natural aura of Rooster people; gladiolas boost steady career growth and continuous progress; impatiens help calm the nerves and relieves stress. Growing and setting these flowers in daily living spaces can not only adorn the environment, but also gather positive fortune for them.  

### Lucky Directions

Due West, Northeast, and Southwest are the lucky directions for Rooster people.  
  
For office seating, taking a seat in the northeast facing southwest helps maintain career stability. Bedheads are ideally oriented toward the west or northeast to ensure good sleep. For important events such as contract signings and negotiations, prioritizing seats in these three directions can improve the odds of success. The East and North should be avoided whenever possible. For critical matters including choosing a city to settle in and purchasing a property, refrain from selecting locations in these two directions to reduce fortune obstacles.

## Personality of People Born in the Year of the Rooster

According to Chinese zodiac, the personalities of Rooster persons have some connections with the natural instincts and inherent habits of roosters. Roosters crow right on time to welcome dawn, a trait that shows itself in Rooster people as innate punctuality, self-discipline, and diligent motivation. Their upright posture and spirited bearing correspond to people’s pursuit of neat personal images and proper manners. Endowed with natural quick wit and vigilance, roosters’ inherent qualities are mirrored in these people’s flexible thinking and decisive conduct. In addition, Roosters are born competitive, and this characteristic is also reflected in their unwillingness to back down or admit failure easily.  

### Strengths

![Image 3](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Diligent, Self-disciplined, and Highly Responsible: Blessed with a steadfast and earnest disposition, they always keep strict track of time. They wholeheartedly commit to all their obligations, embrace strong personal accountability, and never go through the motions or shift duties onto others.  
![Image 4](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Sharp-witted and Perceptive: Rooster natives are thoughtful and insightful. They handle everything in an orderly and rigorous manner, excel at catching subtle details and arranging matters well. They can always keep both life and work neatly organized, staying calm and reliable in all situations.  
![Image 5](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Confident and Sociable: They possess poised demeanor and pay great attention to personal presence. Endowed with fluent speaking skills and quick responses, they are adept at reconciling interpersonal relations and voicing personal views. Warm and generous in interactions, they readily gain trust and favor from people around them.  

### Weaknesses

![Image 6](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Overly Critical: Being a born perfectionist, they hold rigorous standards for themselves and others alike. Excessive preoccupation with trivial details often puts those around in a constrained state.  
![Image 7](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Outspoken and Blunt: Straightforward speech lacks subtle tact, easily stirring unintended offence among others.  
![Image 8](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Vain and Aggressive: Strong self-esteem fosters an aggressive spirit and a refusal to yield. Deep concern of themselves often leads to stubborn insistence on their own views just to preserve personal dignity.  
![Image 9](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Impetuous and Stubborn: Firm adherence to fixed behavioral principles brings rather rigid mindsets, leaving little willingness to take others’ advice. A tendency to get bogged down in stubborn prejudices deprives flexible tact in handling affairs, while mounting pressure will easily trigger inner restlessness and irritability.  

### Personality of Rooster Men

Born pragmatic doers, they are endlessly energetic and never stay idle. They always take the lead within teams and serve as the most reliable pillar of their families. They scorn empty talk, take immediate action once goals are set, and boast outstanding problem-solving capabilities. Yet they often measure others against their own standards, seldom revealing vulnerability or embracing opposing views. When conflicts arise, they would rather stick to their ground than make compromises, and such excessive self-assertion often drains them physically and mentally.  

### Personality of Rooster Women

Endowed with an inborn sense of order, they can straighten out all chaotic situations in good order. They arrange work tasks and household chores perfectly with effortless ease. Gifted with keen observation, they easily notice overlooked details and subtly sense others’ emotional shifts, turning themselves into the most thoughtful and reliable support for people around them. Yet their pursuit of utter perfection often makes them dwell on trivial matters. Excessive concern over others’ opinions also lays invisible restraints on them, keeping them from living in a relaxed and unrestrained state.  

### Personality of the Rooster Born in Different Years

The traditional Chinese chronological system combines the 12-year zodiac cycle and the 10-year cycle of five elements, namely metal, wood, water, fire, and earth, forming a full grand cycle every sixty years. Hence there exist five different versions of the Year of the Rooster every sixty years. # Year of the Rat

 The Rat is the first of the twelve Chinese zodiac animal signs and marks the beginning of a 12-year cycle. Recent years of the Rat include: 2020, 2008, 1996, 1984, 1972, 1960, 1948… The next year of the Rat will be 2032.  
  
People born in these years are typically quick-witted, adaptable, meticulous, and tend to have good financial luck. In 2026, the overall fortune for those born in the year of the Rat will be unfavorable, and they need to exercise extra caution in all aspects of life.  

## Why Is the Rat the First of the Twelve Zodiac Animals?

There are many interesting stories about why the Rat is the first of the twelve zodiac animals.  
  
One legend tells that during a zodiac ranking competition organized by the Jade Emperor, the Rat cleverly jumped onto the Ox’s back and used the Ox’s strength to race to the front of the pack. As they neared the finish line, the Rat made a final leap and snatched first place.  
  
Another theory holds that the selection of the 12 zodiac animals was based on their active hours. The Rat was chosen as the first of the 12 zodiac animals because it is active from 23:00 to 01:00, which marks the beginning of the day.  
  
Or, you may be interested in this legend: In ancient times, the world was a state of chaos, and the universe had not yet taken shape. It was the Rat that gnawed through this chaos, separating heaven and earth and giving form to the universe. As a result, the Rat is regarded as a hero that creates the world and has been granted a special status.

## Lucky / Unlucky Signs for People Born in Rat Year

Each zodiac sign corresponds to a fixed fundamental element, similar to the elements associated with the twelve Western astrology signs. The fundamental element of the Rat is Water. Based on this attribute, it is believed that certain colors, numbers, and directions can bring either good luck or bad luck to those born in the year of the Rat. For example, earth, typically in the colors of yellow or brown, blocks Water; therefore, yellow and brown are considered unlucky for those born in the year of the Rat. Specifically:  

### 1. Lucky and Unlucky Numbers

Lucky numbers: 2, 3  
Unlucky numbers: 5, 9  
Recommendations: When choosing a phone number, apartment floor, or the number of a license plate, prioritize 2 and 3, and avoid 5 and 9.  

### 2. Lucky and Unlucky Colors

Lucky colors: blue, gold, green  
Unlucky colors: yellow, brown  
Recommendations: Use blue, green, and gold more often in wearing, home decor, and car interiors, and try to avoid using yellow or brown.  

### 3. Lucky Flowers

Lily and African violet are considered lucky flowers for those born in a Rat year. You can place some of these flowers at home or in your office to increase your luck.  

### 4. Lucky Directions

Southeast and northeast are the lucky directions for those with Rat as their Chinese zodiac sign. If you position your bedhead toward either of these directions, you may enjoy a more restful sleep.

## Personality of People Born in the Year of the Rat

As mentioned above, the fundamental element of the Rat zodiac sign is Water, which generally symbolizes wisdom, adaptability, and fluidity. As a result, people born in the year of the Rat are typically naturally intelligent and perceptive. Of course, while they possess endearing strengths, they also have weaknesses to be mindful of: they tend to be suspicious.  
  
![Image 3](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Strengths  
Quick-witted and adaptable: They possess keen observational skills and a strong ability to learn, and usually adapt quickly to new environments.  
Diligent and ambitious: They approach tasks with a positive attitude, have clear goals, and are passionate about both career and life.  
Socially adept: Those born in the year of the Rat are natural diplomats: they are typically articulate and humorous, and integrate well into various social circles.  
  
![Image 4](https://data.travelchinaguide.com/images/background/icon/heading-arrow1.png)Weaknesses  
Overly cautious and somewhat short-sighted: They may sometimes miss opportunities due to overthinking and overanalyzing. Besides, they tend to lack long-term planning, but are in pursuit of short-term gains.  
Stingy and somewhat picky: They are so meticulous about finances and attentive to details in life, and can sometimes come across as picky.  

### Personality of Rat Men

Rat men can think quickly and have a good memory. They are curious about everything, get to the bottom of things, and have a strong thirst for knowledge. Meanwhile, they hold on to their own views but seldom have the courage to take action. Men with the Chinese zodiac Rat sign also attach importance to the family.  

### Personality of Rat Women

Rat women are smart and sensible in life, taking a cue from somebody’s words or facial expressions. They also take a good advantage of their strengths and avoid showing weaknesses. All of those make them considerate and their families could be taken care of. However, they may lack the ability to cope with stress.

## Love Compatibility of the Rat

As mentioned above, people born in the year of the Rat are generally intelligent, attentive, and sensitive. In relationships, they tend to be caring and emotionally devoted, but they often lack a sense of security and tend to overthink. They are drawn to people who are stable, reliable, and provide a sense of security, while they dislike those who are unreliable, inconsistent, or overly self-centered.See the illustrations below, or use our testing tool to check the compatibility for you and your partner!

### The Three Zodiac Signs Most Compatible with the Rat

1. The Ox - The Perfect Match  
People born in a year of the Ox are generally steady, reliable, and emotionally stable, making them a perfect complement to those born in a year of the Rat. In a romantic relationship, the Ox can tolerate the Rat’s sensitivity and suspicion, providing a sense of stability; while the Rat can understand the Ox’s quiet determination, offering support and thoughtfulness.  
  
2. The Dragon - Mutual Admiration  
The Dragon is generally bold and visionary. In a relationship, the Dragon admires the Rat’s intelligence, thoughtfulness, and attentiveness; the Rat looks up to the Dragon’s confidence, charisma, and sense of responsibility.  
  
3. The Monkey - Soul Mate  
Equally intelligent and quick-witted, those born in the year of the Monkey are usually on the same wavelength as Rats, with endless topics to discuss. In a relationship, both of them will feel incredibly relaxed and happy, like best friends. Besides, they will give each other space, yet deeply trusting.  

### Zodiac Signs with Moderate Compatibility with the Rat

People with the Chinese zodiac Rat may experience some friction when paired with another Rat, or with those born in the years of the Tiger, Snake, Rabbit, Dog, or Pig. However, there will also be many heartwarming moments. Generally speaking, their romantic life will be fairly uneventful.  

### The Three Zodiac Signs Least Compatible with the Rat

1. Horse - Most Prone to Conflict  
People with the Rat sign of the Chinese zodiac crave stability and a sense of security, while those born in the year of the Horse love freedom and enjoy novelty. When the Rat and the Horse are together, they often find themselves in cold wars, fail to understand each other, and grow increasingly exhausted as their relationship deepens.  
  
2. Rooster- Significant Differences in Thinking  
When interacting, the Rooster may find the Rat too opportunistic and not down-to-earth enough; the Rat, in turn, may find the Rooster rigid, verbose, and prone to making a mountain out of a molehill. Since neither can fully grasp the other’s way of thinking, friction is likely to arise in their daily lives.  
  
3. Sheep - Wearing Each Other Down  
The conflict between the Rat and the Sheep stems from both partners overthinking and lacking a sense of security. Even the slightest issue can lead to suspicion and cold shoulders, making a long-term and stable relationship difficult.
