**Chan Kong-sang[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-3)** (born 7 April 1954), also known as **Fang Shilong**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-4) and known professionally as **Jackie Chan** and **Sing Lung**,[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-5) is a Hong Kong [martial artist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_arts "Martial arts"), [actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor "Actor") and [filmmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filmmaking "Filmmaking"), known for his [slapstick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slapstick "Slapstick"), acrobatic fighting style, comic timing, and innovative stunts, which he typically performs himself. With [a film career](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan_filmography "Jackie Chan filmography") spanning seven decades, he is regarded as one of the most [iconic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_icon "Cultural icon") and influential martial artists in the history of cinema.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-6)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-7) Films in which he has appeared have grossed over $6 billion worldwide.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-8)

Starting as one of the [Seven Little Fortunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Drama_Academy#The_Seven_Little_Fortunes "China Drama Academy") at the [China Drama Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Drama_Academy "China Drama Academy"), where he was trained in acrobatics, martial arts and acting, Chan entered the Hong Kong film industry as a stuntman before making the transition to acting. His breakthrough came with the action comedy _[Snake in the Eagle's Shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake\_in\_the\_Eagle's\_Shadow "Snake in the Eagle's Shadow")_ (1978). He then starred in similar action comedies such as _[Drunken Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunken\_Master "Drunken Master")_ (1978) and _[The Young Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Master "The Young Master")_ (1980). He made his [directorial debut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_directorial_debuts "List of directorial debuts") with _[The Fearless Hyena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fearless\_Hyena "The Fearless Hyena")_ (1979), which was a box office success. Throughout the 1980s, he was part of the "Three Dragons" along with [Sammo Hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammo_Hung "Sammo Hung") and [Yuen Biao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Biao "Yuen Biao"); the three starred in six Hong Kong films together.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-9)_[Project A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project\_A\_(film) "Project A (film)")_ (1983) saw the official formation of the [Jackie Chan Stunt Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan_Stunt_Team "Jackie Chan Stunt Team") and established Chan's signature style of elaborate, dangerous stunts combined with martial arts and slapstick humor, a style he further developed in a more modern setting with _[Wheels on Meals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheels\_on\_Meals "Wheels on Meals")_ (1984) and _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1985\_film) "Police Story (1985 film)")_ (1985). _[Rumble in the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble\_in\_the\_Bronx "Rumble in the Bronx")_ (1995), which had a successful worldwide theatrical run, brought Chan into the North American mainstream.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Utah-10)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-mojo-11) By the mid-1990s, he was the most popular action movie star in [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasia "Eurasia").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Utah-10)

Chan gained [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") success for portraying Chief Inspector Lee in the American [buddy cop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_cop "Buddy cop") action comedy film _[Rush Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush\_Hour\_(1998\_film) "Rush Hour (1998 film)")_ (1998), a role he reprised in [two sequels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush_Hour_(franchise)#Films "Rush Hour (franchise)"). He went on to work both in American and Chinese films, appearing in the _[Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai\_(film\_series) "Shanghai (film series)")_ film series (2000–2003), _[New Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Police\_Story "New Police Story")_ (2004), _[Rob-B-Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob-B-Hood "Rob-B-Hood")_ (2006), _[Little Big Soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Big\_Soldier "Little Big Soldier")_ (2010), _[Shaolin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaolin\_(film) "Shaolin (film)")_ (2011), and _[The Shadow's Edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Shadow's\_Edge "The Shadow's Edge")_ (2025), among others. _[The Forbidden Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Forbidden\_Kingdom "The Forbidden Kingdom")_ (2008) marked his first collaboration with fellow martial arts star [Jet Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Li "Jet Li"). He has played martial arts mentor [Mr. Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_The_Karate_Kid_and_Cobra_Kai_characters#Additional_adaptations "List of The Karate Kid and Cobra Kai characters") in two _[Karate Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Karate\_Kid\_(franchise) "The Karate Kid (franchise)")_ films, the 2010 remake _[The Karate Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Karate\_Kid\_(2010\_film) "The Karate Kid (2010 film)")_ and _[Karate Kid: Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate\_Kid:\_Legends "Karate Kid: Legends")_ (2025). For _[CZ12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12 "CZ12")_ (2012), he earned two _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness\_World\_Records "Guinness World Records")_ for "Most Stunts Performed by a Living Actor" and "Most Credits in One Movie". He played [against type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typecasting#Playing_against_type "Typecasting") in _[Shinjuku Incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku\_Incident "Shinjuku Incident")_ (2009) and _[The Foreigner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Foreigner\_(2017\_film) "The Foreigner (2017 film)")_ (2017).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-13) His voice acting work includes all three Chinese versions of _[Mulan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulan\_(1998\_film) "Mulan (1998 film)")_ (1998), the first three films in the _[Kung Fu Panda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung\_Fu\_Panda "Kung Fu Panda")_ franchise (2008–2016), and _[Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage\_Mutant\_Ninja\_Turtles:\_Mutant\_Mayhem "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem")_ (2023).

One of the most recognizable and influential film personalities in the world, Chan was described by film scholar Andrew Willis in 2004 as perhaps "the most recognized star in the world."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-willis-14) He has received fame stars on the [Hong Kong Avenue of Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avenue_of_Stars,_Hong_Kong "Avenue of Stars, Hong Kong") and the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-16) as well as an [honorary Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") in 2016. Chan has been referenced in various pop songs, films, television series, and video games. He has an award named after him, the [Jackie Chan Action Movie Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan_Action_Movie_Awards "Jackie Chan Action Movie Awards"). He is an operatically trained vocalist who has released [several pop music albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan_discography "Jackie Chan discography") and performed theme songs for some of the films in which he starred. He is also a philanthropist and was named one of the top 10 most charitable celebrities by _[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")_ in 2011.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-17)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Ron_Gluckman-18) In 2016, _Forbes_ ranked him the second-highest-paid actor in the world.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-ChMandle-19)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-20)

## Early life

Chan was born on 7 April 1954 in [British Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Hong_Kong "British Hong Kong") as Chan Kong-sang[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Biography-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-WSJ_20130117-2) to [Charles and Lee-lee Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_and_Lee-lee_Chan "Charles and Lee-lee Chan"), political refugees from the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War"). In circa 1937, Chan's father, originally named Fang Daolong, briefly worked as a secret agent for Lieutenant General [Dai Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dai_Li "Dai Li"), the chief spy in [Kuomintang-ruled China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_government "Nationalist government").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-official_documentary-21) For fear of being arrested by the communist government, Chan's father fled to British Hong Kong in the 1940s and changed his surname from Fang to Chan. Chan was his wife Chan Lee-lee's surname. Chan discovered his father's identity and adopted **Fang Shilong** (房仕龍) as his [Chinese name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_name "Chinese name") in the late 1990s, the name he would have been named according to his kin's [genealogy book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genealogy_book "Genealogy book"), which allegedly traces back to [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") statesman [Fang Xuanling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fang_Xuanling "Fang Xuanling"). Chan's [ancestral roots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_home_(Chinese) "Ancestral home (Chinese)") are located in [Wuhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhu "Wuhu"), [Anhui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anhui "Anhui").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-22)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-23)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-24)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Iamjc-25)

Chan spent his formative years within the grounds of the French consul's residence in the [Victoria Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Peak "Victoria Peak"), British Hong Kong, as his father worked as a cook there.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Tiscali-26) Chan attended the Nah-Hwa Primary School on [Hong Kong Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Island "Hong Kong Island"), where he failed his first year, after which his parents withdrew him from the school. In 1960, his father emigrated to [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra "Canberra"), Australia to work as the head cook for the American embassy, and Chan was sent to the [China Drama Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Drama_Academy "China Drama Academy"), a [Peking Opera School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schools_for_Chinese_opera "Schools for Chinese opera") run by Master [Yu Jim-yuen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Jim-yuen "Yu Jim-yuen").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Tiscali-26)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-CelebValues-27) Chan trained rigorously for the next decade, excelling in martial arts and acrobatics.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-28) He eventually became part of the [Seven Little Fortunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Drama_Academy#The_Seven_Little_Fortunes "China Drama Academy"), a performance group made up of the school's best students, gaining the stage name Yuen Lo (元樓) in homage to his master. Chan became close friends with fellow group members [Sammo Hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammo_Hung "Sammo Hung") and [Yuen Biao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Biao "Yuen Biao"), and the three of them later became known as the _Three Brothers_ or _Three Dragons_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-29) After entering the film industry, Chan along with Sammo Hung got the opportunity to train in [hapkido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hapkido "Hapkido") under the grand master Jin Pal Kim, and Chan eventually attained a [black belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_belt_(martial_arts) "Black belt (martial arts)").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Jackie_Chan's_Hapkido_Master-30) As a martial artist, Chan is also skilled in multiple forms of [Kung fu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_martial_arts "Chinese martial arts").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-31) He is also known to have trained in other martial art forms such as Karate, Judo, Boxing, [Taekwondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taekwondo "Taekwondo"), and [Jeet Kune Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeet_Kune_Do "Jeet Kune Do").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-32)

Chan joined his parents in Canberra, Australia in 1971, where he briefly attended [Dickson College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickson_College "Dickson College") and worked as a construction worker.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-33) A fellow builder named Jack took Chan under his wing, thus earning Chan the nickname of "Little Jack",[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Iamjc-25) later shortened to "Jacky". In the 1980s, the spelling of his nickname became "Jackie", which has stuck with him ever since.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-34)

## Film career

Main article: [Jackie Chan filmography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan_filmography "Jackie Chan filmography")

### 1962–1975: Early small appearances

He began his film career by appearing in small roles at the age of five as a child actor. At age eight, he appeared with some of his fellow "Little Fortunes" in the film _[Big and Little Wong Tin Bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_and\_Little\_Wong\_Tin\_Bar "Big and Little Wong Tin Bar")_ (1962) with [Li Li-Hua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Li-Hua "Li Li-Hua") playing his mother. The following year, the young actor appeared in extras of Yen Chun's 1964 film _Liang Shan Po and Chu Ying Tai_ and had a small role in [King Hu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Hu "King Hu")'s 1966 film _[Come Drink with Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come\_Drink\_with\_Me "Come Drink with Me")_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-35) In 1971, after an appearance as an extra in another kung Fu film, _[A Touch of Zen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Touch\_of\_Zen "A Touch of Zen")_, Chan was signed to Chu Mu's Great Earth Film Company.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Whoami-36)

Chan appeared in the [Bruce Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lee "Bruce Lee") film _[Fist of Fury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fist\_of\_Fury "Fist of Fury")_ (1972), both as an extra and as a [stunt double](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stunt_double "Stunt double") for the Japanese villain Hiroshi Suzuki (portrayed by [Chikara Hashimoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chikara_Hashimoto "Chikara Hashimoto")), particularly during the final fight scene where Lee kicks him and he flies through the air.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-37)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Havis-38) Chan again appeared in another Bruce Lee film, _[Enter the Dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enter\_the\_Dragon "Enter the Dragon")_ (1973), as a minor henchman who gets killed by Lee's character. Sammo Hung helped Chan get minor roles in both of the Bruce Lee films.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-39) Chan also worked as a martial arts choreographer for [John Woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Woo "John Woo")'s _[The Young Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Dragons "The Young Dragons")_ (1974).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Havis-38)

### 1976–1980: Start-up leading roles

In 1976, Jackie Chan received a telegram from [Willie Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Chan "Willie Chan"), a film producer in the Hong Kong film industry who had been impressed with Jackie's stunt choreography work. Willie Chan offered him an acting role in a film directed by [Lo Wei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lo_Wei "Lo Wei"). Lo saw Chan's performance in the [John Woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Woo "John Woo") film _[Hand of Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand\_of\_Death\_(1976\_film) "Hand of Death (1976 film)")_ (1976) and planned to model him after [Bruce Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lee "Bruce Lee") with the film _[New Fist of Fury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Fist\_of\_Fury "New Fist of Fury")_.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Whoami-36) His stage name was changed to 成龍 (literally "becoming the dragon",[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-official_documentary-21)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-WSJ_20130117-2)_Sing4 Lung4_ in [Jyutping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jyutping "Jyutping")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-WSJ_20130117-2) or rarely as _Cheng Long_ in [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_pinyin "Mandarin pinyin")),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-40) to emphasize his similarity to Bruce Lee, whose stage name meant "Lee the Little Dragon" in Chinese. (Note that "dragon" in Lee's name referred to Lee's birth year being the [Dragon zodiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon_(zodiac) "Dragon (zodiac)"), not the [Chinese dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_dragon "Chinese dragon").) The film was unsuccessful because Chan was not accustomed to Lee's martial arts style. Despite the film's failure, Lo Wei continued producing films with similar themes, but with little improvement at the box office.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-FightingMaster-41)

Chan's first major breakthrough was the 1978 film _[Snake in the Eagle's Shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake\_in\_the\_Eagle's\_Shadow "Snake in the Eagle's Shadow")_, shot while he was loaned to Seasonal Film Corporation under a two-picture deal.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Jcm-42) Director [Yuen Woo-ping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Woo-ping "Yuen Woo-ping") allowed Chan complete freedom over his stunt work. The film established the comedic kung fu genre, and proved refreshing to the Hong Kong audience.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-43) The same year, Chan then starred in _[Drunken Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunken\_Master "Drunken Master")_, which finally propelled him to mainstream success.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-44)

Upon Chan's return to Lo Wei's studio, Lo tried to replicate the comedic approach of _Drunken Master_, producing and also showed new features at the time with Jackie as the Stunt Director _[Half a Loaf of Kung Fu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half\_a\_Loaf\_of\_Kung\_Fu "Half a Loaf of Kung Fu")_ and _[Spiritual Kung Fu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual\_Kung\_Fu "Spiritual Kung Fu")_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Iamjc-25) He also gave Chan the opportunity to make his directorial debut in _[The Fearless Hyena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fearless\_Hyena "The Fearless Hyena")_. When Willie Chan left the company, he advised Jackie to decide for himself whether or not to stay with Lo Wei. During the shooting of _[Fearless Hyena Part II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless\_Hyena\_Part\_II "Fearless Hyena Part II")_, Chan broke his contract and joined [Golden Harvest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_Sky_Golden_Harvest "Orange Sky Golden Harvest"), prompting Lo to blackmail Chan with [triads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triad_(organized_crime) "Triad (organized crime)"), blaming Willie for his star's departure. The dispute was resolved with the help of fellow actor and director [Jimmy Wang Yu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Wang_Yu "Jimmy Wang Yu"), allowing Chan to stay with Golden Harvest.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Jcm-42)

### 1980–1987: Commercial success in the action comedy genre

Willie Chan became Jackie's personal manager and firm friend, and remained so for over 30 years. He was instrumental in launching Chan's international career, beginning with his first forays into the American film industry in the 1980s. His first Hollywood film was _[The Big Brawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Big\_Brawl "The Big Brawl")_ in 1980.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-45)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-46) Chan then played a minor role in the 1981 film _[The Cannonball Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cannonball\_Run "The Cannonball Run"),_ which grossed over US$100 million worldwide.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Rovin-47) Despite being largely ignored by North American audiences in favour of established American actors such as [Burt Reynolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burt_Reynolds "Burt Reynolds"), Chan was impressed by the [outtakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outtake "Outtake") shown at the [closing credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_credits "Closing credits"), inspiring him to include the same device in his future films.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

After the commercial failure of _[The Protector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Protector\_(1985\_film) "The Protector (1985 film)")_ in 1985, Chan temporarily abandoned his attempts to break into the US market, returning his focus to [Hong Kong films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_Hong_Kong "Cinema of Hong Kong").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-FightingMaster-41)

Back in Hong Kong, Chan's films began to reach a larger audience in East Asia, with early successes in the lucrative Japanese market including _Drunken Master_, _[The Young Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Master "The Young Master")_ (1980) and _[Dragon Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon\_Lord "Dragon Lord")_ (1982).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-japan-48)_The Young Master_ went on to beat previous box office records set by [Bruce Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lee "Bruce Lee") and established Chan as Hong Kong cinema's top star. With _Dragon Lord_, he began experimenting with elaborate [stunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stunt "Stunt") action sequences,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-:1-49) including the final fight scene where he performs various stunts, including one where he does a back flip off a loft and falls to the lower ground.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-:2-50)

Chan produced a number of action comedy films with his opera school friends [Sammo Hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammo_Hung "Sammo Hung") and Yuen Biao. The three co-starred together for the first time in 1983 in _[Project A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project\_A\_(film) "Project A (film)"),_ which introduced a dangerous stunt-driven style of martial arts that won it the Best Action Design Award at the third annual [Hong Kong Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Film_Award "Hong Kong Film Award").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-51) Over the following two years, the "Three Brothers" appeared in _[Wheels on Meals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheels\_on\_Meals "Wheels on Meals")_ and the original _[Lucky Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucky\_Stars "Lucky Stars")_ trilogy.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-52)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-53) In 1985, Chan made the first _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1985\_film) "Police Story (1985 film)")_ film, a [crime action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_action "Crime action") film in which Chan performed a number of dangerous stunts. It won [Best Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Film_Award_for_Best_Film "Hong Kong Film Award for Best Film") at the [1986 Hong Kong Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_Hong_Kong_Film_Awards "5th Hong Kong Film Awards").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-54) In 1986, Chan played "Asian Hawk", an [Indiana Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_(character) "Indiana Jones (character)")-esque character, in the film _[Armour of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_(film) "Armour of God (film)")._ The film was Chan's biggest domestic box office success up to that point, grossing over HK$35 million.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-55)

### 1988–1998: Acclaimed film sequels and Hollywood breakthrough

In 1988, Chan starred alongside [Sammo Hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammo_Hung "Sammo Hung") and Yuen Biao for the last time to date in the film _[Dragons Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragons\_Forever "Dragons Forever")_. Hung co-directed with [Corey Yuen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corey_Yuen "Corey Yuen"), and the villain in the film was played by [Yuen Wah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuen_Wah "Yuen Wah"), both of whom were fellow graduates of the China Drama Academy.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Chan starred in a number of successful sequels beginning with _[Project A Part II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project\_A\_Part\_II "Project A Part II")_ and _[Police Story 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_2 "Police Story 2")_, which won the award for Best Action Choreography at the 1989 [Hong Kong Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Film_Award "Hong Kong Film Award"). This was followed by _[Armour of God II: Operation Condor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_II:\_Operation\_Condor "Armour of God II: Operation Condor")_, and _[Police Story 3: Super Cop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_3:\_Super\_Cop "Police Story 3: Super Cop")_, for which Chan won the Best Actor Award at the 1993 [Golden Horse Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horse_Film_Festival_and_Awards "Golden Horse Film Festival and Awards"). In 1994, Chan reprised his role as [Wong Fei-hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wong_Fei-hung "Wong Fei-hung") in _[Drunken Master II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunken\_Master\_II "Drunken Master II")_, which was listed in _[Time Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")'_ s All-Time 100 Movies.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-56) Another sequel, _[Police Story 4: First Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_4:\_First\_Strike "Police Story 4: First Strike")_, brought more awards and domestic box office success for Chan, but did not fare as well in foreign markets.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-57)

By the mid-1990s, he was the most popular action movie star in Asia and Europe.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Utah-10) Up until January 1995, his films had grossed over HK$500 million (US$70 million) in Hong Kong[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-58) and ¥39 billion (US$415 million) in Japan,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-japan-48) while having sold over 33 million box office admissions in France, Germany, Italy and Spain up until then.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-boxofficestory-59) Despite his international success, he was not very successful in North America, where he had only two wide releases as a leading actor, _The Big Brawl_ and _The Protector_, grossing US$9.51 million (US$32 million adjusted for inflation).[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-bom-60) Despite this, there was a thriving North American [home video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_video "Home video") market for Chan's Hong Kong films by the mid-1990s.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-61)

Chan rekindled his [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_of_the_United_States "Cinema of the United States") ambitions in the 1990s, but refused early offers to play villains in Hollywood films to avoid being [typecast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typecasting "Typecasting") in future roles. For example, [Sylvester Stallone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_Stallone "Sylvester Stallone") offered him the role of Simon Phoenix, a criminal in the futuristic film _[Demolition Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demolition\_Man\_(film) "Demolition Man (film)")_. Chan declined and the role was taken by [Wesley Snipes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesley_Snipes "Wesley Snipes").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-62)

Chan finally succeeded in establishing a foothold in the North American market in 1995 with a worldwide release of _[Rumble in the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble\_in\_the\_Bronx "Rumble in the Bronx")_, attaining a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") in the United States that was rare for Hong Kong movie stars.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-63) The success of _Rumble in the Bronx_ led to a 1996 release of _Police Story 3: Super Cop_ in the United States under the title _Supercop_, which grossed a total of US$16,270,600. Chan's first huge blockbuster success came when he co-starred with [Chris Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Tucker "Chris Tucker") in the 1998 [buddy cop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_cop "Buddy cop") action comedy _[Rush Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush\_Hour\_(1998\_film) "Rush Hour (1998 film)")_,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-64) grossing US$130 million in the United States alone.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Jcm-42) This film made him a Hollywood star, after which he wrote his autobiography in collaboration with [Jeff Yang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Yang "Jeff Yang") entitled _[I Am Jackie Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Am\_Jackie\_Chan "I Am Jackie Chan")_.

### 1999–2007: Fame in Hollywood and dramatization

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Jackie_Chan_2002.jpg/250px-Jackie_Chan_2002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackie_Chan_2002.jpg)

Chan on the [USS _Kitty Hawk_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Kitty_Hawk_(CV-63) "USS Kitty Hawk (CV-63)") in 2002 during the carrier's visit to Hong Kong[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-65)

In 1998, Chan released his final film for Golden Harvest, _[Who Am I?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who\_Am\_I%3F\_(1998\_film) "Who Am I? (1998 film)")_. After leaving Golden Harvest in 1999, he produced and starred alongside [Shu Qi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shu_Qi "Shu Qi") in _[Gorgeous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgeous\_(film) "Gorgeous (film)")_, a romantic comedy that focused on personal relationships and featured only a few martial arts sequences.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-66) Although Chan had left Golden Harvest in 1999, the company continued to produce and distribute for two of his films, _Gorgeous_ (1999) and _[The Accidental Spy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Accidental\_Spy "The Accidental Spy")_ (2001). Chan then helped create a [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation "PlayStation") game in 2000 called _[Jackie Chan Stuntmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie\_Chan\_Stuntmaster "Jackie Chan Stuntmaster")_, to which he lent his voice and performed the motion capture.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-67) He continued his Hollywood success in 2000 when he teamed up with [Owen Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Wilson "Owen Wilson") in the [Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_(genre) "Western (genre)") action comedy _[Shanghai Noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai\_Noon "Shanghai Noon")_. A sequel, _[Shanghai Knights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai\_Knights "Shanghai Knights")_ followed in 2003 and also featured his first on-screen fight scene with [Donnie Yen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donnie_Yen "Donnie Yen").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-68)

In 2001, Chan planned to make an action comedy titled _[Nosebleed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact\_of\_the\_September\_11\_attacks\_on\_the\_entertainment\_industry#Cancelled\_films "Impact of the September 11 attacks on the entertainment industry"),_ about a window washer working at the [World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") who foils a terrorist plot.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-69) The film was due to begin filming on September 11, but did not enter production before [the attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-70) He reunited with Chris Tucker for _[Rush Hour 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush\_Hour\_2 "Rush Hour 2")_ (2001), which was an even bigger success than the original, grossing $347 million worldwide.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-71) Chan experimented with the use of special effects and wirework for the fight scenes in his next two Hollywood films, _[The Tuxedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tuxedo "The Tuxedo")_ (2002) and _[The Medallion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Medallion "The Medallion")_ (2003), which were not as successful critically or commercially.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-72) In 2004, he teamed up with [Steve Coogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coogan "Steve Coogan") in _[Around the World in 80 Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around\_the\_World\_in\_80\_Days\_(2004\_film) "Around the World in 80 Days (2004 film)")_, loosely based on [Jules Verne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Verne "Jules Verne")'s novel [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around_the_World_in_Eighty_Days "Around the World in Eighty Days"). In 2004, film scholar Andrew Willis stated that Chan was "perhaps" the "most recognized star in the world".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-willis-14)

Despite the success of the _Rush Hour_ and _Shanghai Noon_ films, Chan became frustrated with Hollywood over the limited range of roles and lack of control over the filmmaking process.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Obio-73) In response to Golden Harvest's withdrawal from the film industry in 2003, Chan started his own film production company, [JCE Movies Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCE_Movies_Limited "JCE Movies Limited") (Jackie Chan Emperor Movies Limited) in association with Emperor Multimedia Group (EMG).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Jcm-42) His films have since featured an increasing number of dramatic scenes while continuing to succeed at the box office; examples include _[New Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Police\_Story "New Police Story")_ (2004), _[The Myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Myth\_(film) "The Myth (film)")_ (2005) and _[Rob-B-Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob-B-Hood "Rob-B-Hood")_ (2006).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-74)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-75)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-76)

Chan's next release was the third instalment in the _Rush Hour_ film series directed by [Brett Ratner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Ratner "Brett Ratner"): _[Rush Hour 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush\_Hour\_3 "Rush Hour 3")_ in August 2007. It grossed US$255 million.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-77) However, it was a disappointment in Hong Kong, grossing only HK$3.5 million during its opening weekend.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-78)

### 2008–present: New experiments and change in acting style

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Jackie_Chan_2012_Jelgava.jpg/250px-Jackie_Chan_2012_Jelgava.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackie_Chan_2012_Jelgava.jpg)

Chan on the set of _Chinese Zodiac_, 2 May 2012

Filming of _[The Forbidden Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Forbidden\_Kingdom "The Forbidden Kingdom")_, Chan's first on-screen collaboration with fellow Chinese actor [Jet Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Li "Jet Li"), was completed on 24 August 2007 and the movie was released in April 2008. The movie featured heavy use of effects and wires.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-79)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-80) Chan voiced Master [Monkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kung_Fu_Panda_characters#Monkey "List of Kung Fu Panda characters") in _[Kung Fu Panda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung\_Fu\_Panda\_(film) "Kung Fu Panda (film)")_ (released in June 2008), appearing with [Jack Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Black "Jack Black"), [Dustin Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dustin_Hoffman "Dustin Hoffman"), and [Angelina Jolie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelina_Jolie "Angelina Jolie").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-81) In addition, he has assisted [Anthony Szeto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antony_Szeto "Antony Szeto") in an advisory capacity for the writer-director's film _Wushu_, released on 1 May 2008. The film stars [Sammo Hung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammo_Hung "Sammo Hung") and Wang Wenjie as father and son.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-82)

In November 2007, Chan began filming _[Shinjuku Incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku\_Incident "Shinjuku Incident")_, a dramatic role featuring no martial arts sequences with director [Derek Yee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Yee "Derek Yee"), which sees Chan take on the role of a Chinese immigrant in Japan.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-83) The film was released on 2 April 2009. According to his blog, Chan discussed his wishes to direct a film after completing _Shinjuku Incident_, something he has not done for a number of years.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-84) The film was expected to be the third in the Armour of God series, and had a working title of _[Armour of God III: Chinese Zodiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12 "CZ12")_. The film was released on 12 December 2012.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-85) Because the Screen Actors Guild did not go on strike, Chan started shooting his next Hollywood movie _[The Spy Next Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Spy\_Next\_Door "The Spy Next Door")_ at the end of October in [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-86) In _The Spy Next Door_, Chan plays an undercover agent whose cover is blown when he looks after the children of his girlfriend. In _[Little Big Soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little\_Big\_Soldier "Little Big Soldier")_, Chan stars alongside [Leehom Wang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leehom_Wang "Leehom Wang") as a soldier in the [Warring States period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warring_States_period "Warring States period") in China. He is the lone survivor of his army and must bring a captured enemy soldier Leehom Wang to the capital of his province.

In 2010, he starred with [Jaden Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaden_Smith "Jaden Smith") in _[The Karate Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Karate\_Kid\_(2010\_film) "The Karate Kid (2010 film)")_, a remake of [the 1984 original](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Karate_Kid "The Karate Kid").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-87) This was Chan's first dramatic American film. He plays Mr. Han, a [kung fu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung_fu "Kung fu") master and maintenance man who teaches Jaden Smith's character kung fu so he can defend himself from school bullies. His role in _The Karate Kid_ won him the Favorite Buttkicker award at the [Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickelodeon_Kids'_Choice_Awards "Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards") in 2011.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-88) In Chan's next movie, _[Shaolin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaolin\_(film) "Shaolin (film)")_, he plays a supporting role as a cook of a temple instead of one of the major characters.

His 100th movie, _[1911](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911\_(film) "1911 (film)")_, was released on 26 September 2011. Chan was the co-director, executive producer, and lead star of the movie.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-89) While Chan has directed over ten films over his career, this was his first directorial work since _[Who Am I?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who\_Am\_I%3F\_(1998\_film) "Who Am I? (1998 film)")_ in 1998. _1911_ premiered in North America on 14 October.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-90)

While at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival, Chan announced that he was retiring from action films citing that he was getting too old for the genre. He later clarified that he would not be completely retiring from action films, but would be performing fewer stunts and taking care of his body more.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-91)

In 2013, Chan starred in _[Police Story 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_2013 "Police Story 2013")_, a reboot of the _Police Story_ franchise directed by [Ding Sheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Sheng_(director) "Ding Sheng (director)"), and it was released in China at the end of 2013. Chan's next film _[Dragon Blade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon\_Blade\_(film) "Dragon Blade (film)")_ was released in early 2015 and co-starred Hollywood actors [John Cusack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cusack "John Cusack") and [Adrien Brody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrien_Brody "Adrien Brody"). In 2015, Chan was awarded the title of "[Datuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_titles#Datuk "Malay titles")" by Malaysia as he helped Malaysia to boost its tourism, especially in [Kuala Lumpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuala_Lumpur "Kuala Lumpur") where he previously shot his films.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-92)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-93) In early 2017, Chan's new film titled _[Kung Fu Yoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung\_Fu\_Yoga "Kung Fu Yoga")_, a Chinese-Indian project, which also starred Indian actors [Disha Patani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disha_Patani "Disha Patani"), [Sonu Sood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonu_Sood "Sonu Sood") and [Amyra Dastur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amyra_Dastur "Amyra Dastur"), was released. The film reunited Chan with director [Stanley Tong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Tong "Stanley Tong"), who directed a number of Chan's films in the 1990s. Upon release, the film was a huge success at the box office, and became the 5th highest-grossing film in China, one month after its release.

In 2016, he teamed up with[Johnny Knoxville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Knoxville "Johnny Knoxville") and starred in his own production _[Skiptrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiptrace\_(film) "Skiptrace (film)")_. That same year he also starred in the action-comedy _[Railroad Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad\_Tigers "Railroad Tigers")_. In 2017, he co-starred with [Pierce Brosnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierce_Brosnan "Pierce Brosnan") in the action-thriller _[The Foreigner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Foreigner\_(2017\_film) "The Foreigner (2017 film)")_, an Anglo-Chinese production. He also starred in the 2017 science fiction film _[Bleeding Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleeding\_Steel "Bleeding Steel")_.

In 2018, he served as an executive producer for the plant-based documentary, _[The Game Changers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Game\_Changers "The Game Changers")_, along with [James Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cameron "James Cameron"), [Arnold Schwarzenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger"), and [Pamela Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pamela_Anderson "Pamela Anderson").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-nytgc-94)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-variety-8mar2018-95)

He teamed up with [John Cena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cena "John Cena") and starred in the 2023 Chinese-American co-production _[Hidden Strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden\_Strike "Hidden Strike")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He also voiced [Splinter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splinter_(character) "Splinter (character)") in the animated film _[Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage\_Mutant\_Ninja\_Turtles:\_Mutant\_Mayhem "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem")_.

His films had collectively grossed HK$1.14 billion (US$147 million) at the Hong Kong box office up until 2010,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-96) over US$72 million in South Korea between 1991 and 2010,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-korea2-97) and ¥48.4 billion (US$607 million) in Japan up until 2012.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-japan-48) In Europe, his films collectively sold about 84 million tickets between 1973 and 2010.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-boxofficestory-59)As of 2021[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackie_Chan&action=edit), his films have grossed over [CN¥](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renminbi "Renminbi")14 billion (US$2.17 billion) in China,[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-98) and US$1.84 billion[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-numbers-99) (more than US$2.44 billion adjusted for inflation) in the United States and Canada.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-bom-60)As of 2018[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackie_Chan&action=edit), 48 of his films have collectively grossed more than US$5 billion at the worldwide box office.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-numbers-99)

### Views on filmmaking

On 10 August 2025, during a Q&A session at the [Locarno Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locarno_Film_Festival "Locarno Film Festival"), Chan stated that he believes contemporary Hollywood productions have "lost quality" due to major studios prioritizing profit over creative filmmaking.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-100) He commented, "Right now, a lot of big studios, they're not filmmakers, they're business guys.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-101) They invest 40 million and think, 'How can I get it back?' It's very difficult to make a good movie now.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-102)" Chan contrasted modern productions with what he considered higher-quality films from earlier decades and said his own career goal had been to serve as a "cross-cultural bridge" between the United States and China.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-103)

## Other works

### Music

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Jackie_Chan_and_a_female_singer_2.jpg/250px-Jackie_Chan_and_a_female_singer_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackie_Chan_and_a_female_singer_2.jpg)

Chan and [Qin Hailu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_Hailu "Qin Hailu") singing in Shanghai, China in August 2006

Chan had vocal lessons while at the Peking Opera School in his childhood. He began producing records professionally in the 1980s and has gone on to become a successful singer in Hong Kong and Asia. He has released 20 albums since 1984 and has performed vocals in Cantonese, Mandarin, Japanese, Taiwanese and English. He often sings the theme songs of his films, which play over the [closing credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closing_credits "Closing credits"). Chan's first musical recording was "Kung Fu Fighting Man", the theme song played over the closing credits of _[The Young Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Master "The Young Master")_ (1980).[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-104) At least 10 of these recordings have been released on soundtrack albums for the films.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Nps-105)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Rbb-106) His Cantonese song "Story of a Hero" (英雄故事) (theme song of _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1985\_film) "Police Story (1985 film)")_) was selected by the [Royal Hong Kong Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Hong_Kong_Police "Royal Hong Kong Police") and incorporated into their recruitment advertisement in 1994.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-107)

Chan voiced the character of Shang in the Chinese release of the [Walt Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Pictures "Walt Disney Pictures") animated feature _[Mulan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulan\_(1998\_film) "Mulan (1998 film)")_ (1998). He also performed the song "I'll Make a Man Out of You", for the film's soundtrack. For the US release, the speaking voice was performed by [BD Wong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B.D._Wong "B.D. Wong") and the singing voice was done by [Donny Osmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donny_Osmond "Donny Osmond"). He also collaborated with Ani DiFranco on "Unforgettable".[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-108)

In 2007, Chan recorded and released "We Are Ready", the official one-year countdown song to the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") which he performed at a ceremony marking the one-year countdown to the [2008 Summer Paralympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Paralympics "2008 Summer Paralympics").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-109) Chan also released one of the two official Olympics albums, _Official Album for the Beijing 2008 Olympic Games– Jackie Chan's Version_, which featured a number of special guest appearances.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-110) Chan performed "Hard to Say Goodbye" along with [Andy Lau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Lau "Andy Lau"), [Liu Huan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Huan "Liu Huan") and [Wakin Chau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakin_Chau "Wakin Chau"), at the [2008 Summer Olympics closing ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics_closing_ceremony "2008 Summer Olympics closing ceremony").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-TVB-beijing-111)

### Academia

Chan received his honorary Doctorate of Social Science degree in 1996 from the [Hong Kong Baptist University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Baptist_University "Hong Kong Baptist University").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-School_of_Hotel_and_Tourism_Management,_the_Hong_Kong_Polytechnic_University-112) In 2009, he received another honorary doctorate from the [University of Cambodia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambodia "University of Cambodia"),[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-jackiechan.com-113)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Press2009-114) and has also been awarded an honorary professorship by the [Savannah College of Art and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah_College_of_Art_and_Design "Savannah College of Art and Design") in Hong Kong in 2008.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-China_Daily-115)

Chan is currently a faculty member of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the [Hong Kong Polytechnic University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Polytechnic_University "Hong Kong Polytechnic University"),[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-The_Hong_Kong_Polytechnic_University-116) where he teaches the subject of tourism management. As of 2015[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jackie_Chan&action=edit), he also serves as the Dean of the Jackie Chan Film and Television Academy under the [Wuhan Institute of Design and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan_Institute_of_Design_and_Sciences "Wuhan Institute of Design and Sciences").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-academylaunch-117)

## Personal life

In 1981, Chan met Taiwanese actress [Joan Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Lin "Joan Lin"). In December 1982, they married in Los Angeles; their son, [Jaycee Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaycee_Chan "Jaycee Chan"), was born the day after.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Obio-73) Lin retired from acting after their marriage, but made a cameo in _[CZ12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12 "CZ12")_ (2012), in which she plays Chan's wife.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Chan had an extramarital affair with [Elaine Ng Yi-Lei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaine_Ng "Elaine Ng"), who gave birth to their daughter, Etta Ng Chok Lam, on 18 January 1999. Shortly before Etta's birth, Ng publicly revealed Chan as the father, sparking a scandal. Chan held a press conference where he expressed regret over the affair but stated that he had "only committed a fault that many men in the world commit".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-118)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-119)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-120) In 2002, Ng moved from Hong Kong to Shanghai. She and her daughter attracted media attention for their financial struggles, family conflicts, and mental health issues. However, in 2017 according to her lawyer, Chan refused to provide any assistance.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-121)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-122)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-123)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-124) Chan has never met his daughter since her birth.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-125) In 2017, when asked about her coming out as lesbian, he replied: "As long as she's happy."[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-126)

Chan speaks [Cantonese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantonese "Cantonese"), [Mandarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Chinese "Standard Chinese"), English, [Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language") and [Taiwanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwanese_Hokkien "Taiwanese Hokkien"). He also knows [American Sign Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Sign_Language "American Sign Language").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-127) Chan is an avid [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") fan and supports the [Hong Kong national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_national_football_team "Hong Kong national football team"), the [England national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team"), and [Manchester City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_City_F.C. "Manchester City F.C.").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-128) In January 2026, he revealed that he has [attention deficit hyperactivity disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_deficit_hyperactivity_disorder "Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder") (ADHD).[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-129)

He is a fan of the Italian duo [Bud Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Spencer "Bud Spencer") and [Terence Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence_Hill "Terence Hill"), from whom he was inspired for his movies.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-130)

## Stunts and screen persona

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/US_Navy_021202-N-0271M-016_Jackie_Chan_tries_on_a_fighter_pilot%27s_helmet_with_night_vision_goggles_attached_during_his_visit_aboard_USS_Kitty_Hawk_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-US_Navy_021202-N-0271M-016_Jackie_Chan_tries_on_a_fighter_pilot%27s_helmet_with_night_vision_goggles_attached_during_his_visit_aboard_USS_Kitty_Hawk_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Navy_021202-N-0271M-016_Jackie_Chan_tries_on_a_fighter_pilot's_helmet_with_night_vision_goggles_attached_during_his_visit_aboard_USS_Kitty_Hawk_(cropped).jpg)

Jackie Chan tries on a fighter pilot's helmet with night vision goggles.

Chan has performed most of his own stunts throughout his film career, which are choreographed by the [Jackie Chan Stunt Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan_Stunt_Team "Jackie Chan Stunt Team"). The team was established in 1983, and Chan has used them in all his subsequent films to make choreographing easier, given his understanding of each member's abilities.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-131) Chan and his team undertake many of the stunts performed by other characters in his films, shooting the scenes so that their faces are obscured.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Newline-132)

In the early 1980s, Jackie Chan began experimenting with elaborate stunt action sequences in films such as _[The Young Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Master "The Young Master")_ (1980)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-scmp-133) and especially _[Dragon Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon\_Lord "Dragon Lord")_ (1982),[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-:1-49) which featured a pyramid fight scene that holds the record for the most [takes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take "Take") required for a single scene, with 2900 takes,[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Amazon-134) and the final fight scene where he performs various stunts, including one where he does a backflip off a [loft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft "Loft") and falls to the lower ground.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-:2-50) In 1983, _[Project A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project\_A\_(film) "Project A (film)")_ saw the official formation of the Jackie Chan Stunt Team and added elaborate, dangerous stunts to the fights and typical slapstick humor; at one point, Chan falls from the top of a clock tower through a series of fabric canopies. Critics have compared his comedic stunts in _Project A_ to [Buster Keaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Keaton "Buster Keaton"), who was also known to perform his own stunts, although Chan himself had not watched Keaton's films until years after _Project A_ released; according to Chan, _Project A_ was an evolution of the action stunt work he had been doing in earlier kung Fu comedy films since _The Young Master_.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-scmp-133)

_[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(1985\_film) "Police Story (1985 film)")_ (1985) contained many large-scale action scenes, including an opening sequence featuring a [car chase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_chase "Car chase") through a [shanty town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanty_town "Shanty town"), Chan stopping a [double-decker bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-decker_bus "Double-decker bus") with his service [revolver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pistol "Pistol") and a climactic fight scene in a shopping mall. This final scene earned the film the nickname "Glass Story" by the crew, due to the huge number of panes of [sugar glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_glass "Sugar glass") that were broken. During a stunt in this last scene, in which Chan slides down a pole from several stories up, the lights covering the pole had heated it considerably, resulting in Chan suffering [second-degree burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burn#Classification_by_degree "Burn"), particularly to his hands, as well as a back injury and dislocation of his pelvis upon landing.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-I_Am_Jackie_Chan-135) Chan performed similarly elaborate stunts in numerous other films, such as several _[Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police\_Story\_(film\_series) "Police Story (film series)")_ sequels, _[Project A Part II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project\_A\_Part\_II "Project A Part II")_, the _[Armour of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_(film) "Armour of God (film)")_ series, _[Dragons Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragons\_Forever "Dragons Forever")_, _[Drunken Master II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunken\_Master\_II "Drunken Master II")_, _[Rumble in the Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumble\_in\_the\_Bronx "Rumble in the Bronx")_, and the _[Rush Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rush\_Hour\_(franchise) "Rush Hour (franchise)")_ series, among others.

The dangerous nature of his stunts makes it difficult to get insurance, especially in the United States where his stunt work is contractually limited.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Newline-132) Chan holds the [Guinness World Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") for "Most Stunts by a Living Actor", which emphasizes that "no insurance company will underwrite Chan's productions in which he performs all his own stunts".[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-136)

Chan has been injured frequently when attempting stunts; many of them have been shown as outtakes or as [bloopers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blooper "Blooper") during the closing credits of his films. He came closest to death filming _Armour of God_ when he fell from a tree and fractured his skull. Over the years, he has dislocated his pelvis and also broken numerous parts of his body, including his fingers, toes, nose, both cheekbones, hips, sternum, neck, ankle, and ribs.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-137)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-138) Promotional materials for _Rumble in the Bronx_ emphasized that he performed all of the stunts, and one version of the movie poster even diagrammed his many injuries.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Jackie_Chan_Cannes_2013.jpg/250px-Jackie_Chan_Cannes_2013.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jackie_Chan_Cannes_2013.jpg)

Jackie Chan at the [2013 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Cannes_Film_Festival "2013 Cannes Film Festival")

Chan created his screen persona as a response to the late [Bruce Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lee "Bruce Lee") and the [numerous imitators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruceploitation "Bruceploitation") who appeared before and after Lee's death. Lee's characters were typically stern, morally upright heroes. In contrast, Chan plays well-meaning, slightly foolish regular men, often at the mercy of their friends, girlfriends, or families, who always triumph in the end despite the odds.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Iamjc-25) Additionally, he has stated that he deliberately styles his movement to be the opposite of Lee's: where Lee held his arms wide, Chan holds his tight to the body; where Lee was loose and flowing, Chan is tight and choppy. Despite the success of the _Rush Hour_ series, Chan has stated that he is not a fan of it since he neither appreciates the action scenes in the movie nor understands American humor.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-139)

American filmmaker [Quentin Tarantino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino") classified Chan's style of acting and filmmaking as [physical comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_comedy "Physical comedy"), and considered him one of the greatest in the genre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Utah-10) British filmmaker [Edgar Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Wright "Edgar Wright") describes Jackie Chan as an "expressive" visual performer with an [everyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman "Everyman") persona. He notes that, in contrast to other action heroes (such as Bruce Lee, [Sylvester Stallone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_Stallone "Sylvester Stallone"), [Clint Eastwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Eastwood "Clint Eastwood") or [Arnold Schwarzenegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger "Arnold Schwarzenegger")), Chan presents himself as a loveable "goofball" underdog who overcomes the odds with almost "superhuman" acrobatic stunts and fighting abilities.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Wright-140)

In the 2000s, the ageing Chan grew tired of being typecast as an action hero, prompting him to act with more emotion in his latest films.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-141) In _[New Police Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Police\_Story "New Police Story")_ (2004), he portrayed a character suffering from alcoholism and mourning his murdered colleagues.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Nps-105) To further shed the image of a "nice guy", Chan played an antihero for the first time in _[Rob-B-Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob-B-Hood "Rob-B-Hood")_ (2006) starring as Thongs, a burglar with gambling problems.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-142) Chan plays a low-level gangster in 2009's _[Shinjuku Incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinjuku\_Incident "Shinjuku Incident")_, a serious drama set in Tokyo about unsavory characters.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-143)

Chan has received global recognition for his film acting and stunt work. Reviewers of _Rush Hour 2_, _The Tuxedo_, and _Shanghai Knights_ noted the toning down of Chan's fighting scenes, citing less intensity compared to his earlier films.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-147)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-148)[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-149) The comedic value of his films is questioned; some critics stating that they can be childish at times.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-150) Chan was awarded the [Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (MBE) in 1989 and the [Silver Bauhinia Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Bauhinia_Star "Silver Bauhinia Star") (SBS) in 1999.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-151)[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-152)

When American filmmaker [Quentin Tarantino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino") presented Chan with the Lifetime Achievement Award at the [1995 MTV Movie Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MTV_Movie_Awards "1995 MTV Movie Awards"), Tarantino described Chan as "one of the best filmmakers the world has ever known" and "one of the greatest [physical comedians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_comedy "Physical comedy") since sound came into film."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-Utah-10)

In 2001, he was inducted into the [Martial Arts History Museum Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_Arts_History_Museum "Martial Arts History Museum").[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-153)

He was also awarded an honorary black belt by the [World Karate Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Karate_Federation "World Karate Federation"), along with his _[Karate Kid: Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate\_Kid:\_Legends "Karate Kid: Legends")_ co-star [Ralph Macchio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Macchio "Ralph Macchio") during the film's New York premiere in 2025.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan#cite_note-wkf-154)

## What is my Chinese Zodiac Year Animal?

Chinese people associate each animal sign with **certain characteristics**. It's believed that people born in a given year have the personality of that year's animal.

For example, if you're born after January 27 in 1998, your Chinese zodiac sign is the Tiger as 1998 was a year of the Tiger (beginning at Chinese [New Year](https://www.chinahighlights.com/travelguide/chinese-zodiac/years.htm#)).

_**CZ12**_ ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"):十二生肖; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"):_Shí-èr Shēngxiāo_), also known as _**Armour of God III: Chinese Zodiac**_ and _**Chinese Zodiac**_,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-6) is a 2012 [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film "Action film")[adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_film "Adventure film")[comedy film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_film "Comedy film") co-written, co-produced and directed by [Jackie Chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Chan "Jackie Chan"), who also starred as the main character in the film.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-variety-7) A Chinese-Hong Kong co-production, the film is the third film of a franchise that began with _[Armour of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_(film) "Armour of God (film)")_ (1986) and its sequel, _[Armour of God II: Operation Condor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armour\_of\_God\_II:\_Operation\_Condor "Armour of God II: Operation Condor")_ (1991).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-variety-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-hr-review-8) The film co-stars [Kwon Sang-woo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwon_Sang-woo "Kwon Sang-woo"), [Liao Fan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_Fan "Liao Fan"), [Zoe Zhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Lanxin "Zhang Lanxin"), [Anna Yao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Yao "Helen Yao") and [Laura Weissbecker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Weissbecker "Laura Weissbecker").

The plot follows treasure hunter JC (Chan) and his team who set out on a global quest to find a set of [Chinese zodiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_zodiac "Chinese zodiac") bronze heads that were stolen from a Beijing palace in the 19th century. Released on 20 December 2012, the film went on to gross over US$145 million at the Chinese box office and US$171 million worldwide with mixed-to-negative reviews from critics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-9) The film won Best Stunt Action Choreography for Chan at the [32nd Hong Kong Film Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32nd_Hong_Kong_Film_Awards "32nd Hong Kong Film Awards").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-10) Chan also earned two _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness\_World\_Records "Guinness World Records")_ with the film for "Most Stunts Performed by a Living Actor" and "Most Credits in One Movie".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-TwitchFilm-11)

A sequel, and the fourth film in the _Armour of God_ series, _Armour of God IV: Ultimatum_, is expected to be released in 2027.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CZ12#cite_note-12)
